Questions 1-7 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an opinion essay published in a town newspaper a month before a town meeting vote on whether to charge residents for trash collection by the bag. The paragraphs are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer, the towns, and the figures are invented.)

[1] In Harlow, you pay for water by the gallon and for electricity by the kilowatt-hour, and the more you use, the more you pay. Trash is the exception. Whether a household puts out one bag a week or six, the cost is folded into the property tax, and every household pays the same. At next month's town meeting, voters will decide whether to change that by charging two dollars for each large bag the town collects. I expect the proposal to lose. Eight years ago, I would have voted against it too.

[2] At the time I lived in Dunmore, forty miles north, and when Dunmore adopted the same system, I was one of its loudest critics. I have three children, and I was sure that a per-bag fee was a tax on families like mine, dressed up as an environmental program. Within a year, my household went from five bags a week to two. We had not become virtuous. We had simply started to notice what we threw away, because for the first time throwing it away cost something we could see.

[3] My family was not unusual. In the two years after Dunmore adopted per-bag pricing, the tonnage of trash the town sent to the landfill fell by 38 percent, while the tonnage it recycled rose by nearly half. Two nearby towns that adopted the system later, Pell and Easton, reported declines in landfill tonnage of 31 and 35 percent. Because Dunmore pays the landfill by the ton, its disposal costs fell by more than 200,000 dollars a year, money the town used to lower its property tax rate.

[4] The most common objection to the proposal is that people who do not want to pay for bags will simply dump their trash in the woods or in the bins behind the grocery store. That objection deserves a straight answer, and the straight answer is that it happened. In Dunmore's first six months, the public works department logged more than twice as many reports of illegal dumping as in the same months a year earlier. But the reports fell back to their old level by the end of the first year, after the town posted cameras at the worst sites and fined the handful of repeat offenders it caught. Dumping is a real cost of the change. It is a temporary one, and it can be managed.

[5] The objection I take more seriously is the one I once made myself: that a per-bag fee falls hardest on the households least able to pay it. A family of six produces more trash than a retired couple, no matter how careful it is, and two dollars a bag is a larger share of a small income than of a large one. Here the proposal before the town is weaker than it should be. It offers no discount of any kind.

[6] That can be fixed without abandoning the idea. Dunmore gives every household that qualifies for the state's heating assistance program fifty free bags a year, and it gives families with children in diapers twenty-five more. The program costs the town about a tenth of what it saves at the landfill. Harlow could do the same, and the proposal can be amended on the floor of the town meeting to require it.

[7] Some voters will say that the town should not try to change how people behave, only collect what they throw out. But the current system already changes how people behave: it tells every household that what it throws away costs nothing, and we have behaved accordingly. The question is not whether the price of trash will shape our habits. It is whether the price will be honest. I will vote for per-bag pricing, and I will stand up at the meeting to ask that it come with the discount. I hope enough of my neighbors will do the same.

parts.q:
Which of the following best states the thesis that the essay as a whole defends?
(A) Per-bag pricing reduces the amount of trash a town sends to its landfill, as the experience of Dunmore, Pell, and Easton shows.
(B) Harlow's voters will probably reject per-bag pricing next month, just as the writer herself would have done eight years ago.
(C) Harlow should adopt per-bag pricing, and the proposal should be amended to protect the households least able to pay.
(D) Per-bag pricing is fair only when it includes discounts, so the proposal as it is now written should be voted down.
parts.a: (C). The essay does not state its whole thesis until its last paragraph, and then only as the writer's own plan. Paragraphs 2 to 4 argue that per-bag pricing works and that its costs can be managed; paragraphs 5 and 6 argue that the proposal needs a discount; and paragraph 7 joins the two ('I will vote for per-bag pricing, and I will stand up at the meeting to ask that it come with the discount'). Only (C) holds both halves. (A) is a supporting claim from paragraph 3, one step in the line of reasoning rather than the position it arrives at. (B) is a prediction from paragraph 1, which the essay argues against. (D) overweights paragraph 5: the writer calls the proposal 'weaker than it should be,' but she says she will vote for it and asks that it be amended, not defeated.
parts.n: CLE-1.J (a thesis need not be a single sentence), skill 3.B. Thinking: assemble the overarching claim from the parts of the essay and reject claims that are only steps toward it. Trap: (A), a real claim of the essay that is a step, not the thesis.

parts.q:
The writer's account of her own household in paragraph 2 primarily serves to
(A) show, through a former critic, how a per-bag fee changes what people throw away, which prepares for the town-wide figures in paragraph 3
(B) prove that per-bag pricing reduces the trash of every household, including large families with children like the writer's
(C) establish that the writer's family was already more careful about waste than most of the other families living in Dunmore
(D) concede that the fee is a tax on families with children, a point that the writer accepts again in paragraphs 5 and 6
parts.a: (A). The anecdote illustrates the mechanism the essay depends on, 'for the first time throwing it away cost something we could see,' and it comes from someone who opposed the fee, which makes the change harder to dismiss. Paragraph 3 then opens 'My family was not unusual' and moves from one household to the town's figures, so the anecdote clarifies the statistics that follow. (B) overstates what one household can show; the essay needs paragraph 3 precisely because a single example proves nothing about every household. (C) contradicts the paragraph ('We had not become virtuous') and the next sentence ('My family was not unusual'). (D) confuses the writer's old belief with her present claim: paragraph 2 reports that she once thought the fee was a tax in disguise and then shows why she stopped thinking so; the concern about fairness in paragraph 5 is a different one, about households least able to pay.
parts.n: CLE-1.F (evidence used to illustrate and clarify a point), skill 3.A. Thinking: explain what an anecdote does in a line of reasoning, not just that it is an anecdote. Trap: (B), which asks one story to carry a general claim.

parts.q:
Which of the following conclusions does the evidence in paragraph 3 NOT support without additional information?
(A) Dunmore sent less trash to its landfill in the two years after it adopted per-bag pricing.
(B) Dunmore's results with per-bag pricing were not unique among the towns in its area.
(C) Savings at the landfill helped Dunmore to lower the rate of its property tax.
(D) Most of the trash that Dunmore stopped sending to the landfill was recycled instead.
parts.a: (D). The paragraph gives two percentages, not two amounts. A 38 percent fall in landfill tonnage and a rise of nearly half in recycling tonnage cannot be compared without knowing how much of each there was to begin with: if Dunmore landfilled 8,000 tons and recycled 1,000, the landfill figure fell by about 3,000 tons while recycling rose by only about 500. Some of the missing trash may also have been composted, reduced, or dumped. (A) is stated directly (a 38 percent fall). (B) is supported by the declines in Pell and Easton. (C) is stated directly: the savings were 'money the town used to lower its property tax rate.'
parts.n: CLE-1.B (what evidence can and cannot defend), skill 3.A. Thinking: notice that two percentage changes of different bases cannot be compared as amounts. Trap: (B), because two towns seem too few to generalize from, though 'not unique' needs only one other town with similar results; students miss (D) because 38 percent down and 'nearly half' up look as if they balance.

parts.q:
Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the writer's response to the objection about illegal dumping in paragraph 4?
(A) Dunmore's public works department received more reports of every kind in those first six months, because it had just opened an online reporting form.
(B) After the cameras went up, much of Dunmore's dumping moved to roadsides just past the town line, where it was no longer reported to the town.
(C) Illegal dumping in Dunmore was concentrated at a small number of sites, most of them close to the grocery store and the town's two schools.
(D) The fines Dunmore collected from its repeat offenders did not cover the full cost of buying and installing the cameras at the worst sites.
parts.a: (B). The writer's evidence that dumping was 'temporary' and 'can be managed' is that reports fell back to their old level. If the dumping simply moved beyond the town line, the reports fell because the town stopped seeing it, not because it stopped, and the evidence for her rebuttal no longer shows what she needs it to show. (A) undermines the other half of her paragraph, the concession that dumping doubled; if the rise was partly an artifact of a new reporting form, her case gets stronger, not weaker. (C) is consistent with her account; cameras 'at the worst sites' work best when dumping is concentrated. (D) shows that managing dumping costs money, which the writer never denied; she calls it 'a real cost of the change.'
parts.n: CLE-1.G (evidence must actually support the claim it is chosen for), skill 3.A. Thinking: find the fact that breaks the link between the rebuttal's evidence and its claim. Trap: (A), which attacks the evidence but on the side that helps the writer.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes how the writer's answer to the fairness objection (paragraphs 5 and 6) differs from her answer to the dumping objection (paragraph 4)?
(A) She accepts the fairness objection as a valid criticism of the proposal as written and answers it by amending the proposal, not by disputing it.
(B) She rebuts the fairness objection with evidence from Dunmore, whereas she concedes the dumping objection without offering any evidence at all.
(C) She treats the unfairness of the fee as temporary, like the dumping, and expects that it will disappear by the end of the program's first year.
(D) She dismisses the fairness objection as one she no longer holds, whereas she treats the objection about dumping as a serious and lasting cost.
parts.a: (A). On dumping, the writer concedes a fact and then limits it with evidence that the problem faded (paragraph 4). On fairness, she concedes more: 'Here the proposal before the town is weaker than it should be.' She does not argue that the objection is wrong; she changes her own position to meet it, proposing an amendment modeled on Dunmore's free bags (paragraph 6). (B) reverses the evidence: paragraph 4 gives the dumping reports and their decline, and paragraph 6 uses Dunmore's program to support a remedy, not to rebut the objection. (C) invents a claim; the unfairness is built into the fee, which is why the writer wants a permanent discount. (D) inverts her priorities: she calls fairness 'the objection I take more seriously' and calls dumping 'temporary.'
parts.n: CLE-1.Z (conceding part of a competing claim versus rebutting it), skill 3.C. Thinking: distinguish a concession that limits an objection from one that changes the writer's own proposal. Trap: (B), which mixes up which answer rests on which evidence.

parts.q:
In paragraph 6, the writer claims that Dunmore's discount program 'costs the town about a tenth of what it saves at the landfill.' Which additional information would a voter most need in order to judge whether Harlow could afford the same program?
(A) How many households in Dunmore use all of their free bags each year, and how many use only some
(B) How much Dunmore's property tax rate fell in each of the years after the discount program began
(C) How many Harlow households would qualify, and what Harlow now pays for each ton at its landfill
(D) Whether the Dunmore families who receive free bags recycle more than the families who do not
parts.a: (C). The claim is a ratio from another town: the discount's cost against the landfill savings. Whether it holds for Harlow depends on both sides of that ratio in Harlow, how many households would receive free bags (the cost) and what Harlow pays per ton (which sets the savings). Without them, the Dunmore figure is suggestive but not sufficient. (A) would refine the cost estimate for Dunmore, but it says nothing about Harlow. (B) repeats evidence about Dunmore's savings that the essay already gives and still does not touch Harlow's numbers. (D) is interesting but beside the question of cost; it bears on whether the program changes behavior, not on whether Harlow can pay for it.
parts.n: CLE-1.H (evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality fit the claim), skill 3.A. Thinking: see that a claim borrowed from another town needs the local values of each term before it can support a local decision. Trap: (A), which asks a real question about the wrong town.

parts.q:
Suppose the writer had ended the essay with this sentence: 'The proposal is obviously right, and anyone who votes against it is voting to waste the town's money.' Which best describes how this ending would most likely affect the argument?
(A) It would strengthen the essay, because a forceful final claim leaves readers more confident in the writer's position than a qualified one.
(B) It would make little difference, because the essay's evidence would be the same and readers judge an argument by its evidence alone.
(C) It would strengthen the essay, because it would answer the voters in paragraph 7 who say the town should not try to change behavior.
(D) It would weaken the essay, because it contradicts the writer's own admissions of cost and unfairness and dismisses voters she is trying to win.
parts.a: (D). The essay's credibility rests on its concessions: dumping 'happened,' the proposal is 'weaker than it should be,' and the writer herself once opposed it. An ending that calls the proposal 'obviously right' treats as settled what she has shown is not, and 'anyone who votes against it' insults the very voters, including her past self, whom the essay was written to persuade. (A) assumes that absolute claims persuade better; in an ongoing public debate they usually cost a writer credibility. (B) ignores that readers judge a writer's reasoning and fairness as well as her evidence; the new sentence changes how the evidence reads. (C) mistakes an insult for an answer; the voters in paragraph 7 raise a question about the town's role, and calling them wasteful does not address it.
parts.n: CLE-1.W (effective arguments avoid absolute terms), skill 3.C. Thinking: predict how an absolute, dismissive claim would interact with the concessions the essay has already made. Trap: (A), the belief that certainty always persuades.

Questions 8-13 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an essay published in a city magazine while the city council of Corliss was considering a proposal to install speed cameras on the streets around the city's public schools. The paragraphs are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer, the cities, the people, the organizations, and the figures are invented.)

[1] The argument over speed cameras in Corliss has been conducted almost entirely in the language of money. Supporters point out that the cameras would cost the city nothing, since the company that installs them is paid out of the fines. Opponents call them a tax on commuters dressed up as a safety program. Next month the city council will vote on whether to put cameras on the streets around our eleven public schools, and if the vote is about money, both sides will be able to claim they won. But money is not the point. The point is how fast a car is going when it reaches a child.

[2] Dr. Hana Osei, a trauma surgeon at Corliss Children's Hospital, put it more bluntly than I could. "At twenty miles an hour, I set a broken leg," she said. "At thirty-five, I am talking to the parents in the family room." Walt Pruitt, who has worked as a crossing guard at Garfield Elementary for nineteen years, supports the cameras too, for a reason of his own. "Drivers know where I stand," he told me. "They slow down when they see my vest, and they speed up again the second they're past me. I can't be on every corner."

[3] The best evidence that cameras slow drivers comes from a source I would rather not rely on. Sentry Traffic Systems, the company that would install and run the cameras, commissioned a study of the forty cities it serves and found that speeding at camera sites fell by an average of 63 percent in the first year. A company paid out of the fines has every reason to report that its cameras work, and I would not rest an argument on its numbers alone. But the state transportation department found a similar drop in three cities that bought cameras from other vendors, and I see no reason to doubt the finding. What the study measured, though, was speeding at the cameras. It did not measure crashes, or injuries, or what drivers did a block away.

[4] The case against the cameras has been made mostly by the Corliss Motorists' Alliance, whose pamphlet calls them "a cash grab that has never saved a single life." The pamphlet offers no evidence for that claim, and it never mentions children, pedestrians, or the streets in question; it reads as though the only people on the road were the ones behind the wheel. Still, buried in it is a fair worry. A city that profits from tickets has a reason to want drivers to keep speeding, and a camera program whose revenue grows every year is a program that is failing at its stated purpose.

[5] That worry can be answered without giving up the cameras. The council should approve them for a two-year trial and write three conditions into the ordinance. Every dollar of fine revenue beyond the cost of running the program should go to raised crosswalks, narrower lanes, and wider curbs near the same schools, changes that slow drivers on every corner and not just at the camera. The city should publish, each year, the number of people injured on those streets, not only the number of tickets. And if injuries have not fallen by the end of the trial, the cameras should come down.

[6] I expect the cameras to pass that test. Harmon, an hour south of us, added cameras and raised crosswalks around its schools four years ago, and the number of children injured on those streets has fallen in each year since, from nineteen to seven. Harmon is one city, and four years is a short record. But it is the kind of evidence Corliss should demand of itself.

[7] The Motorists' Alliance is right that a camera can become a tax. It becomes one when a city stops asking what the camera is for. If the council keeps asking, and measures the answer in children who walk home unhurt, the cameras will have earned their place on our corners.

parts.q:
Which best explains why the writer's treatment of the Sentry Traffic Systems study in paragraph 3 is likely to strengthen her credibility with skeptical readers?
(A) She rejects the study's finding because of who paid for it, which shows readers that the camera company cannot sway her.
(B) She names the sponsor's interest, accepts the finding because independent data confirm it, and marks what it did not measure.
(C) She relies on the study as her main evidence that cameras reduce injuries, since even an interested company reports good results.
(D) She accepts the study's finding without any reservation, which shows opponents that she takes their strongest evidence seriously.
parts.a: (B). The writer does three things a skeptic would want: she says plainly why the source might be biased ('A company paid out of the fines has every reason to report that its cameras work'), she accepts the finding only after citing an independent check (the state transportation department's similar result), and she limits what the finding can show ('It did not measure crashes, or injuries'). A reader who distrusts the camera company sees that she distrusts it too, and still has reason to believe the part of the study she uses. (A) contradicts the paragraph: she says 'I see no reason to doubt the finding.' (C) reverses her point; she says the study says nothing about injuries, which is why her proposal in paragraph 5 requires the city to count them. (D) is wrong twice: she accepts the finding with reservations, and the study is not the opponents' evidence; it comes from the company that would profit from the cameras.
parts.n: CLE-1.S (strong arguments acknowledge the biases and limitations of their sources and account for them), skill 3.A. Thinking: judge how acknowledging a source's bias and limits, while still using it, affects a writer's credibility. Trap: (A), the belief that an interested source must be thrown out.

parts.q:
Dr. Osei and Walt Pruitt (paragraph 2) both support the cameras. Which best describes the difference between what each contributes to the writer's argument?
(A) Osei supplies statistical evidence and Pruitt an anecdote, so the two give different kinds of evidence for the very same point.
(B) Osei supports the cameras because they protect children, while Pruitt supports them because they would make his job easier.
(C) Osei speaks as a medical expert and Pruitt as a Garfield parent, so together they represent professional and family concerns.
(D) Osei's experience shows why a car's speed matters to a child who is hit; Pruitt's shows that drivers slow only where watched.
parts.a: (D). The two sources hold the same position from different perspectives. Osei's expertise treating injured children explains what is at stake in a car's speed: the difference between 'a broken leg' and 'the family room.' Pruitt's nineteen years at the curb supply something she cannot: drivers 'slow down when they see my vest' and 'speed up again the second they're past me,' so a person, or a camera, slows traffic only where drivers know they are watched. (A) mislabels Osei's evidence; she gives no statistics, only a vivid contrast drawn from her practice, and the two sources do not make the same point. (B) misreads 'I can't be on every corner,' which is about the limits of what one guard can see, not about easing his work. (C) invents Pruitt's role; he is a crossing guard, and the passage never says he is a parent.
parts.n: CLE-1.R (a position and a perspective are different), skill 3.A. Thinking: separate what two sources on the same side each add, based on who they are and what they have seen. Trap: (A), which sorts evidence by type instead of reading what it shows.

parts.q:
The last two sentences of paragraph 3 ('What the study measured . . . a block away.') serve primarily to
(A) limit what the study can show, preparing for the proposal to count injuries and to slow drivers beyond the cameras
(B) concede that the study undermines the case for cameras, a problem the writer then answers by turning to the pamphlet
(C) suggest that the company designed the study dishonestly, since it had a reason to measure only what would favor it
(D) introduce the Motorists' Alliance's main objection to the cameras, which the writer goes on to accept in paragraph 4
parts.a: (A). These sentences are the writer's commentary on her source: having accepted the finding, she states what it cannot support. The limits she names become the design of her proposal in paragraph 5, which requires the city to publish injuries 'not only the number of tickets' and to spend the revenue on changes 'that slow drivers on every corner and not just at the camera.' The sentences fit the source into her line of reasoning rather than simply reporting it. (B) misreads the move; the study supports the claim that cameras slow drivers, and the sentences only limit its reach. (C) contradicts her stated judgment, 'I see no reason to doubt the finding'; she questions the study's scope, not its honesty. (D) confuses two objections; the Alliance's objection is that the cameras are 'a cash grab,' not that the study measured the wrong thing.
parts.n: CLE-1.L (commentary integrates source material into the line of reasoning), skill 3.A. Thinking: see how commentary on a source's limits sets up the writer's own proposal. Trap: (C), which treats a limit on scope as a charge of dishonesty.

parts.q:
Which best evaluates the writer's treatment of the Motorists' Alliance pamphlet in paragraph 4?
(A) It is unfair, because she dismisses the pamphlet as biased without taking up any of the concerns it raises.
(B) It is unfair, because she criticizes the Alliance's members rather than the argument that the pamphlet makes.
(C) It is fair, because she shows that the pamphlet ignores other positions, yet still answers its one sound concern.
(D) It is fair, because a source that ignores other positions is unreliable and should play no part in the writer's argument.
parts.a: (C). The writer judges the pamphlet by how far it considers other positions: it 'never mentions children, pedestrians, or the streets in question' and offers 'no evidence' for its central claim. But she does not stop there. She finds 'a fair worry' in it, that a city profiting from tickets may want drivers to keep speeding, and she builds her conditions in paragraph 5 to answer it. (A) ignores the second half of the paragraph and all of paragraph 5. (B) mistakes her target: she criticizes what the pamphlet says and leaves out, not the people who wrote it. (D) states the rule the writer declines to follow; a one-sided source is less reliable, but she shows that it can still raise a concern worth answering, and her argument is stronger for answering it.
parts.n: CLE-1.T (how far a source considers other positions reflects its bias), skill 3.A. Thinking: evaluate a writer's handling of a biased source, including the part of it she chooses to accept. Trap: (D), which turns 'biased' into 'worthless.'

parts.q:
The writer wants to cite a source for her claim in paragraph 6 that injuries to children near Harmon's schools fell from nineteen to seven. Which source would give readers the most reason to trust that figure?
(A) A statement by Harmon's mayor, who campaigned for the cameras and won re-election in the year after the program began
(B) The state's database of police-reported injury crashes, searched for the streets near Harmon's schools over those years
(C) Sentry Traffic Systems' report on Harmon, which charts the injuries near each one of the city's schools across eight years
(D) A news story in which Harmon's police chief says that the streets around the city's schools have 'never been safer'
parts.a: (B). A reliable source for this figure is one with no stake in the result and a complete record of the thing being counted. The state's crash database is kept by an agency that neither sold nor championed the program, it records every injury crash reported to police, and readers could check the count themselves. (A) comes from an official whose re-election is tied to the program's success, and a statement is not a record. (C) is the most detailed choice, which is why it tempts, but it comes from the company paid out of the fines, the same interest the writer flagged in paragraph 3; even if Sentry did not run Harmon's cameras, it profits when camera programs look successful. (D) is an interested official's impression, not a count, and it does not give the figure at all.
parts.n: CLE-1.Q (some sources are more reliable or credible than others), skill 3.A. Thinking: weigh a source's interest and the completeness of its record, not just the amount of detail it offers. Trap: (C), eight years of charts from an interested party.

parts.q:
Taken together, Walt Pruitt's observation in paragraph 2 and the limit the writer places on the Sentry study in paragraph 3 most strongly suggest that
(A) cameras will do less to protect children than crossing guards, since a guard can respond to what drivers do and a camera cannot
(B) the Sentry study should not be trusted at all, since a company paid from the fines would design its study to find success
(C) drivers in Corliss are more careless than drivers in the forty cities that the Sentry study examined in its first year
(D) the drop in speeding at camera sites may overstate how much cameras slow drivers along the rest of a child's walk
parts.a: (D). Pruitt reports that drivers slow down where they are watched and 'speed up again the second they're past me.' The writer notes that the Sentry study measured speeding 'at the cameras' and not 'what drivers did a block away.' Combined, the two suggest that a 63 percent drop at the camera may not hold on the streets between cameras, which is exactly why paragraph 5 asks for changes 'that slow drivers on every corner.' (A) compares cameras with guards, but neither source makes that comparison, and Pruitt, who supports the cameras, suggests that guards have the same limit. (B) goes further than the writer, who accepts the finding because the state's data confirm it; the problem the sources point to is scope, not honesty. (C) draws a conclusion about Corliss drivers that no evidence in the passage supports; Pruitt describes how drivers behave near a guard, not how they compare with drivers elsewhere.
parts.n: CLE-1.P (combining evidence from more than one source) with CLE-1.S (accounting for a source's limits), skill 3.A. Thinking: combine a firsthand observation with a study's stated limit to reach a conclusion neither states alone. Trap: (B), which turns a limit of scope into a reason to discard the study.

Questions 14-19 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an opinion essay by a high school civics teacher, published in a city newspaper a month before the Fenwick city council voted on whether to let sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds vote in city elections. The paragraphs are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer, the cities, and the figures are invented.)

[1] For as long as I have taught civics, the argument about lowering the voting age has sounded the same. One side says that sixteen-year-olds are thoughtful and informed, and more serious about the future than the adults who dismiss them. The other side says that sixteen-year-olds are, well, sixteen: impulsive, easily swayed by their parents or their phones, and not yet paying the taxes that elections spend. When the city council takes up the question next month, I expect to hear both speeches again. I have given both of them myself.

[2] I now think both sides are arguing about the wrong thing. The question is not whether sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to vote; some are and some are not, which is also true of forty-year-olds. The question is when a person should cast a first ballot. My answer is that a first vote cast at sixteen, in a city election, is more likely to become a lifelong habit than a first vote cast at eighteen, for reasons of timing, place, and stakes.

[3] Consider timing. Voting, researchers have long observed, is a habit: people who vote in the first election they are eligible for are more likely to keep voting in later ones. Eighteen is close to the worst moment to begin. It is the year when many young people leave home for college, the military, or a first job, and must work out, in an unfamiliar place, how to register, where to vote, and who is on the ballot. At sixteen, most of my students still live at home, a few blocks from their polling place, and they sit in a civics class that could walk them through their first ballot.

[4] Consider place. We do not hand a teenager the car keys on her eighteenth birthday and point her toward the interstate. We give her a learner's permit and let her practice on streets she knows, with someone beside her. A city election is democracy's learner's permit: a shorter ballot, about places a young voter can see, cast in the company of parents who are voting on the same questions.

[5] Consider stakes. The city council decides whether the bus runs past the high school after six o'clock, whether the skate park gets lights, and whether the old armory becomes a teen center or a parking lot. These are not abstractions to a sixteen-year-old. They shape most of the hours a teenager spends outside school, and the people most affected by them have no say in them at all.

[6] The evidence from cities that have tried this is encouraging, though not conclusive. In Kestrel, which lowered its voting age for city elections eight years ago, about one in four registered sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds voted in the first election under the new rule. That sounds low until one notices that among registered voters aged eighteen to twenty-four in the same election, turnout was about one in eight. Kestrel is one city, and its youngest voters may have been stirred by the novelty of the change. But it is the only evidence we have, and it points in one direction.

[7] I am not proposing that sixteen-year-olds vote for president, or for the state legislature, or on the county's bond issues. I am proposing that they vote for the people who decide what happens on their own streets. If the habit takes, Fenwick will have raised a generation of voters. If it does not, we will have lost very little, and we will have learned something the next city can use.

parts.q:
The writer's account of the debate in paragraph 1 primarily serves to
(A) establish that she is a neutral observer of the debate who holds no position of her own on the council's proposal
(B) present her opponents' argument, which she then spends the rest of the essay refuting one point at a time
(C) show that the existing debate turns on maturity, so that she can argue that both sides ask the wrong question
(D) suggest that neither side of the debate has offered any evidence, which is why she turns to Kestrel's figures
parts.a: (C). Paragraph 1 summarizes the conversation the essay is entering: both familiar speeches are about whether sixteen-year-olds are mature. That summary sets up the turn in paragraph 2, 'I now think both sides are arguing about the wrong thing,' and the new question the writer puts in its place, when a first ballot should be cast. 'I have given both of them myself' also shows that she knows both positions from the inside, which makes her reframing harder to dismiss. (A) confuses fairness with neutrality; she takes a clear position in paragraph 2. (B) is wrong on two counts: paragraph 1 presents both sides, not only her opponents', and the essay sets the maturity argument aside rather than refuting it point by point. (D) invents a charge; the writer never says either side lacks evidence, only that both address the wrong question.
parts.n: CLE-1.Y (entering an ongoing conversation means engaging the positions already argued), skill 3.C. Thinking: explain how summarizing a debate prepares a writer to reframe it. Trap: (B), which assumes an opening summary always sets up a rebuttal.

parts.q:
The thesis in paragraph 2 gives 'timing, place, and stakes' as reasons that a first vote at sixteen is more likely to become a habit. Which best evaluates how well paragraph 5 supports that thesis?
(A) It supports the thesis directly, by showing that teenagers who care about local issues will keep voting for the rest of their lives.
(B) It develops the third reason the thesis names, but it argues mainly that teenagers deserve a say, leaving the link to habit unstated.
(C) It supports the thesis by showing that sixteen-year-olds understand the council's decisions and are mature enough to vote on them.
(D) It contradicts the thesis, which claims that city elections make good practice because what they decide matters less than other races.
parts.a: (B). Paragraph 5 does take up 'stakes,' the third reason, and shows that city decisions matter to teenagers. But its final sentence turns to fairness, 'the people most affected by them have no say in them at all,' which is an argument for letting teenagers vote, not an argument that a first vote at sixteen will become a habit. The connection the thesis needs, that a vote on something one cares about is more likely to be cast and repeated, is left for the reader to supply. (A) credits the paragraph with a claim it never makes; nothing in it shows what teenagers will do for the rest of their lives. (C) brings back the maturity question that paragraph 2 explicitly set aside. (D) misstates the thesis; the writer never says city decisions matter less, and paragraph 5 argues the opposite.
parts.n: CLE-1.O (a thesis may preview the line of reasoning), skill 3.B. Thinking: test whether a body paragraph delivers the reason the thesis promised or drifts to a neighboring claim. Trap: (A), which assumes that a paragraph under the right heading supports the thesis.

parts.q:
A reader objects to paragraph 4: 'The learner's permit comparison fails. A learner drives with a licensed adult in the passenger seat, but no adult will stand beside a sixteen-year-old in the voting booth.' Which best evaluates this objection?
(A) It names a real difference, but the writer places the guidance in parents voting on the same ballot, so it limits the analogy without defeating it.
(B) It defeats the comparison entirely, because an analogy is valid only when the two things being compared are alike in each and every one of their respects.
(C) It misses the point, because an analogy is an illustration rather than evidence and so cannot be weakened by an objection to how well it fits.
(D) It is correct but beside the point, because paragraph 4 is a digression from the essay and plays no part in the writer's line of reasoning.
parts.a: (A). The objection is fair as far as it goes: no one supervises the ballot itself. But the writer has already located the supervision elsewhere, in a first vote 'cast in the company of parents who are voting on the same questions,' on a short ballot about 'places a young voter can see.' The comparison still holds at the point that matters to her, which is practice under guidance before the harder test, so the objection limits the analogy rather than breaking it. (B) holds analogies to an impossible standard; every analogy compares things that differ, and the question is whether they differ in the respect the argument depends on. (C) goes too far the other way; an analogy offered as a reason, as this one is, can be judged by how well it fits. (D) ignores the thesis, which names 'place' as one of the three reasons; paragraph 4 is that reason.
parts.n: CLE-1.C (analogy as a type of evidence), skill 3.A. Thinking: judge whether a difference between two compared cases touches the point the analogy is used to make. Trap: (B), the belief that any difference defeats an analogy.

parts.q:
A student summarizes the essay this way: 'The writer argues that teenagers today are mature and informed enough to vote, so the voting age should be lowered to sixteen.' Which best identifies the problem with this summary?
(A) It misstates the writer's position, since she argues that the voting age should stay at eighteen for every kind of election.
(B) It is accurate, but it leaves out the figures from Kestrel, which are the most important evidence the writer offers.
(C) It overstates the writer's confidence, since she admits in paragraph 6 that her evidence for the change is not conclusive.
(D) It brings back the maturity argument she sets aside and drops her limit to city elections, giving her a claim she rejects.
parts.a: (D). The summary reduces a qualified argument to the familiar one the writer says is beside the point. She states that the question 'is not whether sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to vote,' and she limits her proposal to city elections, explicitly excluding president, the legislature, and bond issues (paragraph 7). A summary that bases her case on maturity and lowers the voting age across the board attributes to her a position she argues against. (A) swings too far; she does propose a change, for city elections. (B) calls the summary accurate, which it is not; omitting one piece of evidence would be a small flaw beside misstating the claim. (C) points to a real feature of paragraph 6, but the summary says nothing about how certain she is; its error is what it says she claims, not how confidently.
parts.n: CLE-1.V (a lack of understanding of a subject's complexity leads to oversimplification), skill 3.C. Thinking: compare a summary with the text's qualified claim and name what it distorts. Trap: (C), a true observation about the essay that does not describe the summary's error.

parts.q:
The first sentence of paragraph 7 ('I am not proposing . . . bond issues.') functions mainly to
(A) concede that sixteen-year-olds are not yet mature enough to vote in state and national elections
(B) limit the proposal to elections where her reasons apply and reassure readers wary of a larger change
(C) suggest that city elections matter less than other elections, so that a failed trial would cost little
(D) introduce a second proposal about state and national elections, which the writer will argue for later
parts.a: (B). The sentence narrows the claim's scope. The writer's reasons of place and stakes apply to elections about 'what happens on their own streets,' so she confines the proposal to those, and in doing so she answers in advance the reader who fears that city elections are a first step toward a national change. (A) reintroduces the maturity argument; the writer gives no reason for the limit that has to do with maturity, and she said in paragraph 2 that maturity is not the question. (C) contradicts paragraph 5, which argues that city decisions matter a great deal to teenagers; 'lost very little' refers to the cost of trying the change, not to the importance of the elections. (D) has no basis; the sentence rules those elections out rather than promising to argue for them.
parts.n: CLE-1.X (modifiers and clauses that limit the scope of an argument), skill 3.C. Thinking: explain why a writer narrows a claim and whom the narrowing is for. Trap: (A), which reads a limit of scope as a concession about maturity.

parts.q:
Suppose the writer learned that in Kestrel, residents who first voted at sixteen or seventeen went on to vote in later city elections no more often than residents who first became eligible at eighteen. Which revision would this evidence most require?
(A) Removing the learner's permit comparison in paragraph 4, since the evidence shows that practice does not help new voters
(B) Mentioning the finding in paragraph 6 as a limitation, while keeping the thesis and the rest of the argument as they are
(C) Revising the thesis's central claim about habit, which the finding contradicts, and resting the case more on stakes
(D) Adding detail to paragraph 5 about the council's decisions, since the stakes argument does not depend on turnout
parts.a: (C). The thesis claims that a first vote at sixteen 'is more likely to become a lifelong habit.' The new finding tests exactly that claim in the only city the writer cites, and it fails. A thesis contradicted by the writer's own best evidence has to change; what survives is the argument from stakes, that teenagers are affected by city decisions, which does not depend on habit. (A) removes one illustration but leaves the contradicted claim standing at the center of the essay. (B) looks honest, but a limitation qualifies a claim the evidence still supports; here the evidence refutes it, so a footnote would leave the essay arguing for something the writer knows is not so. (D) strengthens a paragraph that survives the finding but does nothing about the thesis the finding undercuts.
parts.n: CLE-1.U (new evidence may require revising the thesis and the line of reasoning), skill 3.B. Thinking: decide whether new evidence qualifies a claim or overturns it, and revise accordingly. Trap: (B), which treats contradicting evidence as a limitation to acknowledge.

mc.stem:
Questions 20-25 refer to the following.

The following passage is a draft of a letter that a high school junior is writing to the five members of her district's school board, which is considering closing the high school's student-run radio station to save money. Several board members have said publicly that the station serves only the few students who work there. (Written for practice; the writer, the school, the town, and the station are invented.)

(1) Every weekday at 7:40, about three hundred people in Halden tune in to hear students read the school announcements, the lunch menu, and the weather on Halden High Radio. (2) The school board is considering closing the station next year. (3) Last year, forty-one students worked at the station as announcers, reporters, and sound engineers. (4) Several of them now study communications or audio engineering in college. (5) The station's adviser is Mr. Paul Garza. He says, "It teaches students to meet a deadline that doesn't move." (6) During the ice storm in February, when the town's power was out for two days, the station stayed on the air on a generator and read the list of warming centers every hour.

(7) The station costs the district about 22,000 dollars a year, mostly for the adviser's stipend and replacement equipment. (8) Some board members have argued that students can now make podcasts on their phones, so a radio station is no longer necessary. (9) Obviously, a podcast is completely different from a radio station, and anyone who says otherwise doesn't understand radio. (10) According to a survey, 87 percent of students said the station should stay open. (11) In conclusion, the board should not close the station.

parts.q:
The writer wants to replace sentence 2 with a thesis that states her position and indicates the reasons that the rest of the letter develops. Which version best achieves this goal?
(A) The school board is considering closing the station next year, a decision that many students and families in Halden feel strongly about.
(B) The board should keep the station, because it prepares students for college and careers and serves the whole town when it matters most.
(C) The board should keep the station, because radio has been an important part of American history and culture for more than a century.
(D) Closing the station would be a mistake, and in this letter I will explain several reasons why the board should reconsider its plan.
parts.a: (B). This version takes a position that requires defense and names the two reasons the draft goes on to support: training that lasts beyond high school (sentences 3 to 5) and service to the town (sentences 1 and 6). The second reason also answers the board members who say the station serves 'only the few students who work there.' (A) reports the situation without taking a position; no one would need to argue for it. (C) takes a position, but its reason appears nowhere in the letter, so the thesis would promise an argument the draft never makes. (D) announces that reasons exist without saying what they are, so it previews nothing about the line of reasoning.
parts.n: CLE-1.I (a thesis is the main claim the writer defends with reasoning and evidence), skill 4.B. Thinking: choose the thesis that both requires defense and matches the reasons the draft actually develops. Trap: (C), a real claim whose reason the letter never supports.

parts.q:
The writer wants to revise sentence 5 so that the adviser's words are woven into her own sentence and explain why the experience described in sentences 3 and 4 matters. Which version best achieves this goal?
(A) Mr. Paul Garza is the station's adviser, and he says this about it: "It teaches students to meet a deadline that doesn't move."
(B) The station's adviser, Mr. Paul Garza, has many reasons for believing that the station is valuable to the students who work there.
(C) The station teaches students "to meet a deadline that doesn't move," which is true because a live broadcast cannot be paused.
(D) According to the adviser, Mr. Paul Garza, those students learned "to meet a deadline that doesn't move," a habit every job demands.
parts.a: (D). The quoted phrase becomes part of the writer's own sentence, it is attributed to Garza, 'those students' ties it to the forty-one workers in sentence 3, and the closing phrase, 'a habit every job demands,' explains why that lesson matters after high school, which is the point of sentences 3 and 4. (A) still drops the quotation in whole behind a colon and adds no explanation, the problem the writer wants to fix. (B) removes the adviser's actual words and replaces them with a vague claim that he has 'many reasons.' (C) embeds the phrase smoothly, but it drops the attribution, so the reader cannot tell whose words these are, and its commentary explains radio rather than what the students gained.
parts.n: CLE-1.E (syntactically embedding quoted material in one's own ideas), skill 4.A. Thinking: judge a revision by whether the quotation is embedded, attributed, and connected to the writer's point. Trap: (C), smooth embedding without attribution or a link to the claim.

parts.q:
The figure in sentence 10 comes from a survey that the school newspaper, the Halden Crier, conducted in March; 230 of the school's 1,100 students responded. The writer wants to revise sentence 10 to credit the source and to report the figure accurately, so that board members can judge how much weight it deserves. Which version best achieves this goal?
(A) In a March survey by the school paper, the Halden Crier, 87 percent of the 230 students who responded said the station should stay.
(B) According to many students at Halden High School, 87 percent of the student body believes that the station should stay open next year.
(C) According to a recent survey, 87 percent of students, which is nearly everyone, said that the station should stay open next year.
(D) According to the Halden Crier, 87 percent of Halden High School's 1,100 students believe that the station should stay open next year.
parts.a: (A). It names the source and the date, and it reports the figure as what it is, the share of 230 respondents, so a board member can see that about a fifth of the school answered and weigh the number accordingly. (B) attributes the figure to 'many students,' which is not a source, and inflates it into a claim about the whole student body. (C) still hides the source and adds a comment, 'nearly everyone,' that the data do not support. (D) credits the right source, which makes it tempting, but it misreports the figure: 87 percent of 230 respondents is not 87 percent of 1,100 students, and a board member who checked would lose trust in the whole letter.
parts.n: CLE-1.N (acknowledging others' work through attribution), skill 4.A. Thinking: attribute a figure so that the reader knows both where it came from and what it measures. Trap: (D), which names the source but misstates what the number describes.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how the ice storm supports her argument, for board members who believe the station serves only the students who work there. Which sentence best achieves this goal?
(A) The ice storm was among the worst in Halden's history, and many families went without heat or light for two days.
(B) Afterward, many listeners wrote to the school to thank the students who had kept the station on the air that week.
(C) For those two days the station was not an activity for forty-one students but a service to the whole town.
(D) This shows that the students at the station are responsible and dedicated and that they care about their school.
parts.a: (C). The sentence is commentary: it states what the ice-storm evidence proves and aims it at the board's belief, turning 'an activity for forty-one students' into 'a service to the whole town.' (A) adds more detail about the storm without explaining what it shows about the station. (B) is related evidence, and it tempts because it shows listeners valued the station, but it is another fact that still needs explaining, not the explanation the writer wants. (D) is commentary, but it links the evidence to the wrong claim, the students' character, which is not what the board doubts.
parts.n: CLE-1.K (commentary establishes the logical relationship between evidence and claim), skill 4.A. Thinking: tell commentary that links evidence to the disputed claim from more evidence or from commentary aimed at another claim. Trap: (B), strong evidence mistaken for commentary.

parts.q:
The writer wants to revise sentence 9 so that it responds to the board members' argument in sentence 8 by granting what is reasonable in it while keeping her own position. Which version best achieves this goal?
(A) It is true that a podcast teaches many of the same skills, but a podcast is not live and could not have done what the station did in February.
(B) Obviously, podcasts can be useful, but anyone who knows anything about radio knows that a podcast is nothing at all like a real radio station.
(C) It is true that students can now make podcasts on their phones, so perhaps the station is no longer as necessary as it once was for students.
(D) Podcasts may be popular today, but experts agree that radio will always be the most trusted and important form of media in the entire world.
parts.a: (A). It concedes the part of the board members' argument that is true, that a podcast teaches many of the same skills, and then rebuts the rest with the writer's own evidence: a live station did something in the ice storm that a recording could not. The concession makes her sound fair to the readers she is trying to persuade. (B) adds a token concession but keeps the absolute claim and the insult to 'anyone who' disagrees, which includes some of her readers. (C) concedes so much that it gives up her position. (D) replaces the insult with an unsupported appeal to unnamed 'experts' and another absolute claim, 'always.'
parts.n: CLE-1.Z (conceding part of a competing claim and rebutting the rest), skill 4.C. Thinking: find the revision that grants what is true in an objection without surrendering the claim. Trap: (C), a concession that swallows the argument.

parts.q:
The writer wants to replace sentence 4 with evidence that would best convince board members who doubt that working at the station helps students after high school. Which version best achieves this goal?
(A) Several of my friends who work at the station say that they would like to go into radio or journalism someday after college.
(B) Of the ninety-six students who worked at the station in the past five years, twenty-three have gone on to study or work in media.
(C) Radio and podcast companies employ thousands of people across the country, and many of those jobs pay very good salaries today.
(D) Last year the station won second place in a statewide contest for student broadcasters, beating schools twice the size of Halden's.
parts.a: (B). The board's doubt is about what happens to students after high school, and this version answers it with an outcome, measured over five years, with the number of students it is drawn from, so a reader can see both the result and its scale. (A) reports hopes, not outcomes, and comes from the writer's friends, which a skeptical reader will discount. (C) shows that media jobs exist but says nothing about whether the station helps anyone get one. (D) shows that the station is good, which tempts, but a prize measures the quality of the broadcasts, not what the students did afterward.
parts.n: CLE-1.H (evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality fit the claim), skill 4.A. Thinking: match the evidence to the doubt the audience actually holds. Trap: (D), impressive evidence for a different claim.

fr.title: Argument: should one person's story sway a public decision?
fr.stem:
In a newspaper column about how towns decide what to pay for, a retired city budget director wrote the following. (The budget director and the column are invented for practice.)

'I sat through twenty years of public hearings, and I can tell you what wins them. It is not the best spreadsheet. It is the mother at the microphone holding a photograph of her son. People call that a failure of reason. I have come to think it is the opposite: a decision that ignores the people it touches is not rational. It is only tidy.'

Write an essay that argues your position on the role that personal stories should play when a community makes public decisions.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

rows.earns: A defensible position on the role personal stories should play, not merely a verdict that they are good or bad, for example: 'Personal stories should decide which problems a community looks at, but numbers should decide how it responds, because a story can reveal what a statistic hides but cannot tell a council whether it is typical.' A thesis that fully agrees or fully disagrees with the budget director also earns the point when it takes a position that needs defending, such as 'Stories deserve real weight in public decisions, because the people who live with a decision know things no spreadsheet records.' The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear in the introduction or the conclusion.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('Personal stories play an important role in public decisions'); a both-sides statement with no position ('Stories and statistics each have strengths and weaknesses'); a thesis about the budget director rather than the issue ('The budget director makes a good point'); or a claim no one would dispute ('People are moved by emotional stories').

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how that evidence supports the position. Evidence may come from reading, history, current events, or the writer's own experience, for example: residents' accounts at a hearing that sent officials to find a problem their data had missed; a town that put its one new traffic signal at the corner where a well-known student was hurt while the crash records pointed to busier, more dangerous intersections; the well-documented tendency of people to give more to help one named person than to help many unnamed ones; or the fact that people who can attend a 7 p.m. hearing and speak at a microphone are not a random sample of the people a decision touches. For each example, the commentary explains what the story added or distorted, and why that bears on the role stories should play.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence for each claim, but commentary is uneven or sometimes restates the evidence. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly summarizes it or repeats the thesis ('This shows how powerful stories are'). 1: evidence that is general or merely hypothetical, with little explanation ('For example, if a mom tells a sad story, the council might agree with her'). 0: restates the thesis or is irrelevant. An essay built on one invented hypothetical, or on paraphrasing the budget director's column, cannot score above 2.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently identifies and explores a complexity or tension in the issue, for example: that a statistic is itself a count of many people's stories, so the real question is which stories get counted; that a story is most valuable when it reveals what the data missed and most dangerous when it stands in for data about how common a problem is; or that giving weight to stories favors those with the time and confidence to tell them, so a community that values stories must go looking for the ones it does not hear. A consistently vivid and persuasive style can also earn the point.
rows.loses: A single sentence nodding to 'the other side'; a sweeping remark such as 'In today's world, emotion decides everything' that the essay never develops; or a list of examples with no idea connecting them.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that argues a defensible position on the role personal stories should play when a community makes public decisions.
parts.a: Model: 'The budget director is right that stories belong in public decisions but wrong about what they are for: a personal story should tell a community where to look, and the numbers should tell it how large the problem is and where its money will do the most good.' It takes a position that a reasonable reader could dispute, and it previews a line of reasoning: what stories reveal, what they distort, and how the two kinds of evidence should divide the work.
parts.n: 'Personal stories can be very persuasive in public decisions, but statistics are also important' earns nothing: it takes no position on what role stories should play, so there is nothing for the essay to defend.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline a line of reasoning in three body paragraphs, each with specific evidence and the commentary that explains how the evidence supports your position.
parts.a:
¶1 What stories reveal: residents of one street tell a hearing that their basements flood after every storm; the city's flood maps, drawn from river gauges, show no risk there; an engineer sent because of the testimony finds a collapsed storm drain that no map could show. Commentary: the stories did not replace evidence; they told the city where to look for evidence it had never gathered, which is the role they should play.
¶2 What stories distort: a town puts its one new traffic signal at the corner where a well-known student was struck, while the county's crash records show three intersections with far more injuries waiting another year. Commentary: the story was true and the grief was real, but one case cannot tell a council how common a danger is, so the town spent its signal where the story was loudest rather than where the risk was greatest.
¶3 Whose stories are heard: the people who can come to a 7 p.m. hearing, speak easily at a microphone, and bring a photograph are not a random sample of those a decision affects, and people reliably give more to help one named person than many unnamed ones. Commentary: a community that lets the most vivid story win will favor the people best placed to tell it; if stories are to count, the community must seek out the ones it does not hear and test every story against the numbers.
Each example must be one the writer actually knows, named or placed (a town, an article, a hearing she attended); the same incidents offered as 'imagine a town that...' are hypothetical and, as Row B says, cannot score above 2.
parts.n: A plan that lists three examples of moving stories, each followed by 'this shows stories are powerful,' earns at most 2: each paragraph needs commentary on what the story added or distorted and why that bears on the role stories should play.

parts.q: Row C plan: explain how this essay could earn the sophistication point by developing a complexity in the issue rather than simply taking a side.
parts.a: Carry one tension through the essay: the budget director treats the story and the spreadsheet as rivals, but a statistic is a count of many people's stories, and a story is one data point with a face. The essay can then argue that the real danger is not emotion but an unrepresentative sample: the mother at the microphone deserves to be heard, and so do the parents who could not find a babysitter that night. The conclusion can offer a test that follows from this: a story should change a decision when it reveals something the numbers missed, and should not when it merely drowns them out.
parts.n: Ending with 'Of course, there are two sides to every issue' or 'Stories and statistics both matter in their own way' names no complexity and explores nothing, so it earns nothing.

fr.title: Testing the cameras: claims and evidence in the Corliss essay
fr.stem:
The paragraphs below are from the essay on speed cameras near Corliss's schools in questions 8-13. Reread them and answer the questions that follow. (Written for practice; the writer, the cities, the organizations, and the figures are invented.)

[4] The case against the cameras has been made mostly by the Corliss Motorists' Alliance, whose pamphlet calls them "a cash grab that has never saved a single life." The pamphlet offers no evidence for that claim, and it never mentions children, pedestrians, or the streets in question; it reads as though the only people on the road were the ones behind the wheel. Still, buried in it is a fair worry. A city that profits from tickets has a reason to want drivers to keep speeding, and a camera program whose revenue grows every year is a program that is failing at its stated purpose.

[5] That worry can be answered without giving up the cameras. The council should approve them for a two-year trial and write three conditions into the ordinance. Every dollar of fine revenue beyond the cost of running the program should go to raised crosswalks, narrower lanes, and wider curbs near the same schools, changes that slow drivers on every corner and not just at the camera. The city should publish, each year, the number of people injured on those streets, not only the number of tickets. And if injuries have not fallen by the end of the trial, the cameras should come down.

[6] I expect the cameras to pass that test. Harmon, an hour south of us, added cameras and raised crosswalks around its schools four years ago, and the number of children injured on those streets has fallen in each year since, from nineteen to seven. Harmon is one city, and four years is a short record. But it is the kind of evidence Corliss should demand of itself.

[7] The Motorists' Alliance is right that a camera can become a tax. It becomes one when a city stops asking what the camera is for. If the council keeps asking, and measures the answer in children who walk home unhurt, the cameras will have earned their place on our corners.

parts.q: The Motorists' Alliance pamphlet calls the cameras 'a cash grab that has never saved a single life' (paragraph 4). In paragraph 7 the writer says, 'The Motorists' Alliance is right that a camera can become a tax. It becomes one when a city stops asking what the camera is for.' Explain how the writer's version of the Alliance's claim differs from the pamphlet's, and why that difference lets her grant the claim without weakening her own position.
parts.a: The writer turns an absolute claim into a conditional one. The pamphlet says what the cameras are ('a cash grab') and what they have never done ('never saved a single life'), a claim that allows no exceptions and that, she has pointed out, comes with no evidence. Her version says only that a camera 'can become' a tax, and only 'when a city stops asking what the camera is for.' Stated that way, the claim is one she can accept, because her proposal in paragraph 5 is built to keep the city asking: revenue beyond the program's cost goes to street changes near the schools, injuries are published every year, and the cameras come down if injuries do not fall. Granting the narrowed claim shows opponents that she has heard their real concern, and it makes her three conditions the answer to that concern, so the concession ends by supporting her position rather than giving ground.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'she agrees with the other side to seem fair' or 'she uses a counterargument,' which names the move without explaining how narrowing the claim makes it compatible with her own position; or a reading that says she has changed her mind and now opposes the cameras.

parts.q: A council member who supports the cameras reads paragraph 6 and says: 'Harmon proves that speed cameras cut injuries to children by more than half. Corliss will get the same result.' Evaluate the council member's claim, using evidence from the passage.
parts.a: The claim goes further than the evidence allows. The arithmetic is right, since a fall from nineteen to seven is a drop of more than half, but Harmon 'added cameras and raised crosswalks' at the same time, so its record cannot show how much of the decline the cameras caused; the crosswalks, which slow drivers at every crossing and not only where a camera watches, may account for much of it. The second sentence fails for a different reason: Harmon is 'one city' with 'a short record' of four years, and Corliss may differ in its streets, its traffic, and the number of children who walk to school. The writer herself offers Harmon as 'the kind of evidence Corliss should demand of itself,' a model of what to measure rather than proof of what will happen. A defensible version of the claim: 'In one city, cameras together with raised crosswalks were followed by a steep drop in injuries near schools, which is reason to try the same combination here and count the result.'
parts.n: Earns nothing: agreeing because 'the numbers show a big drop'; or disagreeing only because 'the writer says Harmon is one city,' with no account of why one city, or two changes made at once, limits what the figure can show. A response that disputes the arithmetic misreads the problem: nineteen to seven is more than half.

parts.q: The writer's third condition (paragraph 5) is that 'if injuries have not fallen by the end of the trial, the cameras should come down.' A second council member objects: 'That test could take down cameras that are working.' Explain how the test could lead to that result. Then propose one change to the trial, or to the way it is judged, that would make it a fairer test of the cameras, and justify your change.
parts.a: The objection is sound. Injuries to children on the streets near eleven schools are, fortunately, few (Harmon's count began at nineteen), so over a two-year trial the number can stay flat or rise by chance, or because of something the cameras do not control, such as more children walking after a change in school boundaries or a new housing development, even while the cameras are doing what they were installed to do, which is slowing drivers. The street changes paid for by the fines also take time to build, so part of the program may barely be in place when the count is taken. A fairer test compares: judge the injury count near the camera schools against the count on similar streets without cameras, or against the city's injury trend over the same two years, so that a citywide rise or an unlucky year is not blamed on the cameras. The justification is that a test of the cameras has to separate what they do from what would have happened anyway. The point requires both halves: a specific way the test could take down working cameras (small counts that swing by chance, a cause outside the cameras, or street changes not yet built), and one change justified by how it makes the verdict more reliable. The comparison above is one such change; adding a measure that responds within months, such as drivers' speeds a block from each camera, or lengthening the trial so that small counts have time to show a trend, earns the point equally when the response explains why it makes the verdict more reliable.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the test is unfair because two years is short' with no account of why a short period or a small count can mislead; or a change with no justification, or one that measures the wrong thing, such as counting tickets, which measures revenue, the very thing the writer says is not the point.

fr.title: Qualifying a claim: the phone-pouch paragraph
fr.stem:
Last fall, Brenton High School began requiring students to lock their phones in pouches from the first bell to the last. The school board will decide in May whether to keep the policy. A junior who supports it is writing an editorial for the school newspaper, which board members read. Below is one body paragraph of her draft; the sentences are numbered. (Written for practice; the student, the school, the people, and the figures are invented.)

(1) The phone pouches have made Brenton a better place to learn, and every high school in the state should adopt them. (2) In a survey the school conducted in January, 41 of Brenton's 52 teachers said that students were paying closer attention in class than they had the year before. (3) Ms. Adeyemi, who teaches chemistry, told me, "I used to compete with thirty screens. Now I only compete with the clock." (4) "It was annoying for about a week," said sophomore Luis Ferrer. (5) Some students also say they talk to each other more at lunch. (6) The pouches cost the district about eight dollars per student.

The student has also found the district's report on first-semester grades, released in February. It shows that 11 percent of the grades given at Brenton were a D or an F, the same share as in the first semester of the year before. She has not decided whether to mention it.

parts.q: Sentence 1 claims more than the evidence in the paragraph can defend. Rewrite sentence 1 as a qualified claim that this evidence could support, and explain which part of the original claim the evidence cannot defend, and why.
parts.a: Model rewrite: 'In their first semester, the phone pouches seem to have made Brenton's classrooms more attentive, which is reason enough for the board to keep them for another year.' The original overreaches in two ways. 'Every high school in the state' rests on one school's experience; nothing in the paragraph shows how schools of other sizes, or schools with their own phone rules already in place, would fare. And 'a better place to learn' claims an overall result, while the evidence covers one thing, attention in class, reported as the impressions of 41 of 52 teachers after a single semester. The rewrite limits the claim's scope to Brenton, its subject to attention, its time to one semester, and its certainty with 'seem,' so every part of it is something sentences 2 and 3 can defend, and it still takes a position the board has to decide on.
parts.n: Earns nothing: a rewrite that only adds 'I believe' or 'I think' and keeps the unsupported scope; one that qualifies so heavily that it takes no position ('The pouches may or may not help students'); or an explanation that calls the claim 'too strong' without naming what the evidence fails to show.

parts.q: A classmate reviewing the draft advises: 'Leave the grade report out. It doesn't help you, and it only gives the other side ammunition.' Do you agree? Justify your answer with reference to the paragraph's readers and its claim, and explain how the student should handle the grade report.
parts.a: Disagree. The board members who will decide the policy read the newspaper and will have the district's report; an editorial that is silent about it will look either uninformed or evasive, and an opponent will cite the figure anyway. Nor does the report contradict a well-qualified claim. The survey records what teachers see during class, while the grade report counts final results, which depend on much besides attention, and one semester may be too short a time for a change in attention to show up in grades. The student should concede the figure and let it narrow her claim, for example: 'The pouches have not yet raised grades; the share of Ds and Fs was 11 percent in both first semesters. But one semester may be too soon for grades to move, and what 41 of 52 teachers report is the change that would have to come first: students paying closer attention.' Handled this way, the report makes her more credible, and it gives the board a reason to keep the policy long enough to learn whether the attention turns into achievement. The point requires a position, a justification that uses both the readers (board members who will have the report) and the claim (what the report does and does not measure), and a specific way to handle the report. Disagreeing earns it, and a response that places the report in a different paragraph of the editorial counts as disagreeing; agreeing to keep the report out of the editorial earns nothing, however it is argued, because the board will have the report either way.
parts.n: Earns nothing: agreeing because the figure 'weakens the argument,' since evidence that complicates a claim is a reason to qualify the claim, not to hide the evidence from readers who will see it; or disagreeing only because 'writers should include all the evidence,' with no account of how the report can fit the claim.

parts.q: The student's teacher writes beside sentences 4 through 6: 'Each of these is a fact, but none is tied to your claim.' Choose one of the three sentences to keep, and write one or two sentences of commentary that connect it to the claim you wrote in part (a). Then explain why one of the other two should be cut or moved.
parts.a: Keep sentence 4 and follow it with commentary such as: 'Ferrer's complaint is the one readers expect from students, but it lasted a week; the closer attention teachers reported in January had lasted a whole semester, which suggests that the benefit is not a novelty that will fade.' The commentary turns a stray quotation into an answer to an objection the board will raise, that students resent the pouches, and ties it to the claim that the change in attention is worth keeping. Sentence 6 should move: the cost bears on whether the district can afford the pouches, a question the board will ask but a different claim from whether they improve attention, so it belongs in a paragraph about cost. The point requires all three pieces: a kept sentence, commentary that says how that fact supports the part (a) claim, and a reason for cutting or moving one of the other two that names the claim it does or does not serve. Any of the three sentences may be kept. Keeping sentence 6 earns the point when the commentary ties the cost to the claim, for example by arguing that eight dollars a student is a small price for the attention sentence 2 reports; keeping sentence 5 earns it only if the part (a) claim reaches beyond the classroom, since talk at lunch is not attention in class. Cutting sentence 5 is as well justified as moving sentence 6: 'some students' is an unnamed and uncounted source, and talk at lunch is not attention in class.
parts.n: Earns nothing: commentary that restates the sentence ('This shows that Luis found the pouches annoying') or asserts the claim without linking the fact to it ('This proves the pouches work'); or a cut justified only by 'it is off topic,' without saying what claim the sentence does serve.

reo.intro: Every passage and draft is written for practice; the writers, places and figures in them are invented.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-7 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an essay by a retired traffic engineer, published in the opinion section of a regional newspaper. The paragraphs are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer and publication are invented.)
