(D) gives the right prediction for the wrong reason: nothing links a vague promise about the transition to the enrollment figures.
parts.n: RHS-1.N (choosing evidence for this audience), skill 1.B. Thinking: predict how a distrustful audience would hear a vague promise in place of verifiable ones, and why. Trap: (D), the right direction with a reason the passage does not support.

parts.q:
Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the speaker's credibility with this audience?
(A) The speaker grew up in another county and has worked in this school district for only four years.
(B) Enrollment at Carver Street Elementary has also fallen over the last twelve years, though more slowly than Marlow's.
(C) The family council described in paragraph 6 will be able to advise the Carver Street principal but not to overrule her.
(D) The estimate for the roof repair was prepared by a contractor who is bidding to build new classrooms at Carver Street.
parts.a: (D). The 1.4-million-dollar roof estimate is the heaviest figure in paragraph 5, the paragraph that asks the parents to understand the board's choice. If it came from someone who profits from the closing, the figure looks self-serving, and it would confirm the very fear the speaker voiced in paragraph 4, that 'the county seat takes.' (A) contradicts nothing he said: he claims to have attended 'a school like this one,' not one in this county, and his promises do not rest on long service. (B) might raise questions about Carver Street's future, but it touches no statement in the speech, and combining two shrinking schools can still make sense. (C) matches what he actually promised, 'the means to watch' and 'the standing to tell us, in public,' not a veto.
parts.n: RHS-1.H (logos and ethos depend on trusted evidence), skill 1.B. Thinking: find the fact that would undercut the speaker's key evidence and confirm the audience's suspicion at once. Trap: (A), which assumes that any outsider detail damages ethos.

parts.q:
The speech ends with the hope that 'some of the people who signed that petition will be sitting at the table' (paragraph 7). Which best describes how this ending relates to the rest of the speech?
(A) It returns to the petition from paragraph 1 and recasts its signers, once the district's opponents, as the people best placed to hold it to its word.
(B) It sums up the commitments listed in paragraph 3 so that the audience will be able to remember each of them after the meeting has ended.
(C) It concedes that the petition's signers were right all along and that the new council ought to work to reverse the board's decision.
(D) It introduces a new request, that parents serve on the council, which none of the earlier paragraphs has prepared the audience to accept.
parts.a: (A). The petition first appears in paragraph 1 as the parents' fight against the district. In the last sentence the same signers are invited to the table, as the people with the most reason to watch closely, which is exactly the council's job ('the means to watch what we do with your children'). The ending connects to the introduction and turns the audience's opposition into a role. (B) misdescribes the ending, which names only the council's first meeting and repeats none of the commitments. (C) goes beyond the speech: the speaker declines to call the parents wrong, but he never calls the board wrong either, and the council's job is to watch the transition, not to undo it. (D) overlooks paragraph 6, which introduces the council, and the whole speech's emphasis on holding the district 'to our promises.'
parts.n: RHS-1.J (a conclusion that connects to the introduction), skill 1.A. Thinking: trace how the ending changes the meaning of a detail from the opening. Trap: (C), which reads the invitation to the petitioners as a concession on the vote.

mc.stem:
Questions 8-13 refer to the following.

The two passages below were written by the same person, a wildlife biologist employed by Tamsen County, about a proposal to return beavers to Mill Creek, which runs through farmland in the county. Passage 1 is from a memo she sent to the county's board of commissioners. Passage 2 is a letter she mailed a week later to the forty-one families who own land along the creek. The sentences are numbered through both passages. (Written for practice; the writer, the county, and the figures are invented.)

Passage 1

(1) This memo recommends that the county fund a three-year pilot project to return beavers to the upper six miles of Mill Creek. (2) In each of the last four summers, the creek has stopped flowing for three to nine weeks, and the county has spent an average of 86,000 dollars a year hauling water to livestock operations along its banks. (3) Beaver dams slow the release of water from a watershed: in comparable streams in this region, reaches with active beaver colonies have held surface water an average of five weeks longer into late summer than reaches without them. (4) The pilot would cost an estimated 140,000 dollars over three years, most of it for monitoring, flow-control devices, and the relocation of two to four beaver families from sites where they are now trapped as nuisances. (5) The principal risk is localized flooding of fields and culverts. (6) This risk is manageable: a flow-control pipe installed through a dam holds a pond at a fixed height, and in a survey of 300 such installations in neighboring states, 87 percent required no maintenance after their first year. (7) Because every site would be on private land, the project cannot proceed without the landowners' consent, and I expect some of them to be skeptical. (8) I recommend that the board approve the pilot on the condition that written agreements are signed with the affected landowners, and that it direct staff to report the project's results at the end of each year.

Passage 2

(9) Dear Mill Creek neighbor,

(10) By now some of you have heard that the county is thinking about putting beavers back in Mill Creek, and I suspect a few of you said something about the idea that I could not print in a letter. (11) I understand. (12) A beaver can take down a young apple tree in a night, and a dam in the wrong place can put a foot of water on a hayfield. (13) I would not ask you to take on that kind of trouble for a theory.

(14) So let me tell you what I have seen. (15) Two summers ago, in the last week of August, I waded into Harlan Creek over in Bexley County, the same week our own creek was dry enough to walk across. (16) The water came to my knees. (17) The man who owns that stretch of Harlan Creek trapped beavers for thirty years. (18) He keeps them now on purpose, because his cattle have not gone short of water since.

(19) Nothing will happen on your land without your signature. (20) If you sign on, the county will pay for a pipe that keeps each pond from rising past a line you and I mark together, and for wire wrap on any tree you want to keep. (21) If a dam floods a field anyway, a county crew will take it out within forty-eight hours of your call, at no cost to you. (22) If you do not sign, the beavers go somewhere else, and nobody from the county will ask you twice.

(23) On the evening of March 12, I will be at the Grange hall with photographs of Harlan Creek, and with the man who owns it. (24) Come and ask him what I can't answer.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes a difference in how the writer presents the risk of flooding in the two passages?
(A) Passage 1 plays the risk down in order to win the county's funding, while Passage 2 exaggerates it in order to win the landowners' trust.
(B) Passage 1 raises the risk only after giving the project's cost, while Passage 2 waits to raise it until the writer has described Harlan Creek.
(C) Passage 1 treats the risk as a manageable problem backed by data, while Passage 2 names it in the owners' terms and answers it with promises.
(D) Passage 1 makes the landowners responsible for any flood damage, while Passage 2 makes the county responsible for repairing all of that damage.
parts.a: (C). The memo calls flooding 'the principal risk' and answers it with a mechanism and a statistic (sentence 6), which is what a board deciding whether to spend public money needs. The letter names the same risk as the owners would, 'a foot of water on a hayfield' and a lost apple tree (sentence 12), and answers it with promises about their own land: a line 'you and I mark together' and a crew 'within forty-eight hours' (sentences 20 and 21). (A) misreads both passages: the memo names flooding plainly as the principal risk, and the letter's hayfield is concrete, not exaggerated. (B) is half right: the memo does give the cost (sentence 4) before the risk (sentence 5), but the letter raises the risk in sentence 12, before Harlan Creek. (D) invents a difference: the memo never assigns flood damage to the landowners; it requires only their consent (sentences 7 and 8).
parts.n: RHS-1.N (evidence and language chosen for each audience), skill 1.B. Thinking: compare how one writer handles the same fact for two audiences with different needs. Trap: (B), which is accurate about Passage 1 and wrong about Passage 2.

parts.q:
The survey of 300 flow-control installations (sentence 6) appears in Passage 1 but not in Passage 2. Which best explains the writer's choice?
(A) The writer doubts the accuracy of the survey and is willing to use it only with readers whom she expects not to examine it closely.
(B) The landowners would be unlikely to understand a percentage, so the writer replaces the statistic with a simpler story about one creek.
(C) The survey's finding that 13 percent of installations needed further work would contradict the guarantee the writer makes in sentence 21.
(D) The writer judges that owners wary of 'a theory' will trust another owner's experience more than data from other states.
parts.a: (D). Sentence 13 shows that the writer expects these readers to discount anything that sounds like theory, and sentences 14 to 18 answer with what she has seen and with the example of a man who, like them, owns land along a creek and once trapped beavers. The commissioners, who must justify spending, get the survey; the landowners get a neighbor. (A) has it backward: commissioners deciding on public money are the readers most likely to examine the survey, and they are the ones who receive it. (B) rests on a condescending assumption the passage does not support; the letter still uses figures ('a foot of water,' 'forty-eight hours'), and it chooses testimony for trust, not for simplicity. (C) sounds careful but misreads sentence 21, which is written for exactly the cases in which a pipe does not work; the 13 percent is the reason for the guarantee, not a contradiction of it.
parts.n: RHS-1.F (a writer's perception of an audience guides the choice of evidence), skill 1.B. Thinking: explain an omission by what one audience needs and the other distrusts. Trap: (C), which invents a conflict between the statistic and the guarantee.

parts.q:
How does the diction of sentences 10 and 11 most likely affect the way the landowners perceive the writer?
(A) It suggests that the writer finds the landowners' objections amusing, which sets her at a distance from the very people she is writing to.
(B) It shows that she expects and accepts their anger, which presents her as a neighbor who knows them rather than an official with a plan.
(C) It signals that the letter is informal and so less important than the memo, which lowers the stakes of the decision for the reader.
(D) It establishes the writer's expertise as a biologist before she gives her evidence, which the landowners are likely to respect.
parts.a: (B). 'I suspect a few of you said something about the idea that I could not print in a letter' names the readers' likely reaction, in their own register, before they can raise it, and 'I understand' accepts it without argument. A writer who can predict her readers' language sounds like someone who knows them, which matters for readers who are being asked to trust the county with their land. (A) misreads the humor as mockery; the joke is at the expense of her own proposal, and it is followed at once by 'I understand.' (C) confuses an informal register with low stakes; the letter asks for a signature that decides what happens on each reader's land. (D) finds something the sentences do not contain; nothing in them concerns expertise, which is exactly what the letter avoids leading with.
parts.n: RHS-1.L (diction shapes how an audience perceives the writer), skill 1.B. Thinking: explain how an informal, self-deprecating opening changes the writer's standing with a suspicious audience. Trap: (A), which reads humor about the proposal as humor about the readers.

parts.q:
A student argues that Passage 2 is less honest than Passage 1 because the letter leaves out the project's cost and the survey data. Which of the following best evaluates the student's argument?
(A) It is convincing, because a writer who gives one audience evidence that she withholds from another is misrepresenting her project to both.
(B) It is convincing, because the letter replaces evidence with emotional appeals, which are by their nature less honest than statistics.
(C) It is unconvincing, because the letter names the risk plainly, plans for the pipes failing, and lets each owner refuse, so its omissions mislead no one.
(D) It is unconvincing, because the letter does give the project's cost, in the form of the county's promise to pay for the pipes and wire wrap.
parts.a: (C). An omission is dishonest when it leaves readers with a false picture, and the letter leaves none. The commissioners decide whether to spend 140,000 dollars, so they get the cost and the survey. The owners decide whether to allow beavers on their own land, at no cost to them (sentences 20 and 21); the letter tells them plainly what could go wrong (sentence 12), never claims the pipes always work, promises a crew for when they do not (sentence 21), and tells them they can say no (sentences 19 and 22). The two texts share one writer and one message but serve two rhetorical situations. (A) states a rule that would make every audience-aware choice dishonest. (B) treats emotional appeal as dishonest by nature, and overlooks that the letter's Harlan Creek account is evidence: testimony and personal observation. (D) misreads a promise as a figure; the letter never states the project's cost.
parts.n: RHS-1.A (the same message in two rhetorical situations), skill 1.A. Thinking: judge whether an omission is deception or an adjustment to what a different audience must decide. Trap: (A), which sounds principled but rules out adapting to any audience.

parts.q:
Suppose that in Passage 2 the writer had described the risk with the words of sentence 5, 'localized flooding of fields and culverts,' instead of 'a foot of water on a hayfield' (sentence 12). How would the landowners most likely have responded, and why?
(A) More favorably, because precise technical language would show the owners that the writer had studied the problem carefully.
(B) Less favorably, because 'localized' measures the flood from the county's side, where one field is small, and so may belittle their loss.
(C) About the same, because both phrases describe the same risk, and the landowners already know what a flood does to a field.
(D) Less favorably, because the technical phrase would reveal to the owners that the county expects the flooding to be worse than the letter admits.
parts.a: (B). Word choice carries a point of view. To a board looking at six miles of creek, 'localized' is accurate and reassuring: any flooding stays near a dam. To the owner of that field, the flood is not local; it is his hay. With readers already wary of the county, the word could sound like an official calling their loss small, and it would cost the writer the credibility that sentences 10 to 13 were built to earn. (A) assumes technical diction builds credibility with every audience; with readers who distrust 'a theory' (sentence 13), it would do the reverse. (C) treats diction as neutral packaging around a fact; the fact is the same, but its framing from the county's side changes how the owner hears the writer. (D) predicts the right direction for the wrong reason: 'localized' is the milder phrase, not a sign of worse flooding.
parts.n: RHS-1.M (word choice can reveal a writer's vantage and affect credibility), skill 1.B. Thinking: predict how a word that is accurate for one audience would sound to another, and why. Trap: (C), which assumes that two phrases for the same fact have the same effect.

parts.q:
A classmate argues that the letter's last sentence, 'Come and ask him what I can't answer,' weakens the writer's credibility, because it admits that there are questions she cannot answer. Which of the following best evaluates the classmate's argument?
(A) It is convincing, because a writer who admits the limits of her own knowledge gives skeptical readers a reason to doubt the rest of her letter.
(B) It is convincing, because the admission contradicts the certainty with which the writer describes the flow-control pipes in sentence 20.
(C) It is unconvincing, because the sentence is only a closing courtesy, and the final sentence of a letter has little effect on its credibility.
(D) It is unconvincing, because for readers wary of theory, admitting what only experience can answer, and bringing that experience, builds trust.
parts.a: (D). The letter has told us who these readers are: people who will not take on trouble 'for a theory' (sentence 13). For them, a county biologist who claims to know everything would sound like the county; one who admits what only a rancher can answer, and then brings the rancher, sounds like someone who respects what they know. The admission is part of the letter's ethos, not a crack in it. (A) states a general rule that fails for this audience; these readers already doubt confident experts. (B) misreads sentence 20, which says what the county will pay for, not that the pipes never fail; sentence 21 even plans for the cases when they do. (C) dismisses the ending, which ties the letter's evidence (Harlan Creek) to a concrete next step and leaves the readers with a voice they are more likely to believe than hers.
parts.n: RHS-1.D (an audience's shared beliefs decide what reads as credible), skill 1.B. Thinking: judge a claim about credibility by asking what this particular audience trusts. Trap: (A), a rule about ethos that holds for some audiences and fails for this one.

mc.stem:
Questions 14-19 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an essay by a 911 dispatcher, published in a city newspaper during a week in April that many communities set aside to recognize emergency dispatchers. The paragraphs are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer, the city, and the bill are invented.)

[1] The call came in at 2:14 on a Tuesday afternoon, and the first thing I heard was a cartoon. Then a small voice said, "My dad fell down and he won't talk." Her name was Maya. She was six. For the next nine minutes, until the paramedics came through the front door, I was the only adult in that living room who could help her father, and I was eleven miles away.

[2] I have been a 911 dispatcher for sixteen years, and I have taken perhaps two hundred thousand calls. You have probably never thought about me, which is how it should be. Nobody thinks about the dispatcher unless something has gone wrong, and on most days, for most of you, nothing has. But this is the one week a year when cities print proclamations about people like me, and I would like to use it to tell you what the proclamations leave out.

[3] What they leave out is that on Maya's call, I did not just send an ambulance. I taught a six-year-old to tilt her father's head back, to count out loud, and to push on his chest with both hands, hard, while I counted with her. Dispatchers in this state give CPR instructions, talk people out of burning buildings, and keep callers on the line while an intruder is still in the house. We are, in the words of a paramedic I work with, "the first first responders." But in the state's job classifications, we are clerical workers, listed alongside the people who file permits at the county courthouse.

[4] That classification is not a matter of pride. It decides whether dispatchers are trained for the calls we take, whether we are offered counseling after the ones that go badly, and whether we can retire at the same age as the firefighters and officers we send out. Our center is budgeted for thirty-two dispatchers. We have twenty-one. Last year, eight of the people we trained left within eighteen months, most of them for jobs that paid the same and did not wake them at night.

[5] House Bill 212, which the legislature will take up this month, would move dispatchers into the same category as the responders we work beside. Some legislators have said it costs too much, and I will not pretend it is free. But a dispatcher who quits after a year takes her training with her, and it costs this city about forty thousand dollars to train the next one. We are already paying for the turnover. We are just paying for it after the fact.

[6] If you want to do something for dispatchers this week, you do not need to send a card. Call your representative and ask how he or she will vote on House Bill 212. And if you ever have to call us, stay on the line, tell us where you are before you tell us what happened, and do what we ask, even if it seems strange. We cannot see you. We are trying to.

[7] Maya's father lived. I know because she sent a drawing to the center a month later: a stick-figure man, a smiling girl, and a telephone with a long, looping cord. It hangs over my console. The proclamations are nice. The drawing is why I stay.

parts.q:
The essay pursues more than one purpose. Which best describes how its purposes are related?
(A) Its main purpose is to honor dispatchers, and its discussion of House Bill 212 is a digression prompted by the week of recognition.
(B) Its main purpose is to teach readers how to call 911, and the story of Maya's call is an example of a caller who followed instructions.
(C) It uses a week of praise to press for a policy change, and its advice to callers supports its claim that dispatchers do skilled work.
(D) Its purposes are at odds, since the essay asks for readers' support while complaining that the public has never thought about dispatchers.
parts.a: (C). Paragraph 2 announces the plan: to use the week 'to tell you what the proclamations leave out.' What they leave out, the gap between the work and its classification, leads to House Bill 212 and the request in paragraph 6 to call a representative. The practical advice in paragraph 6 ('stay on the line... do what we ask, even if it seems strange') serves both purposes: it helps readers, and it shows again that callers' lives depend on a dispatcher's instructions, the point paragraph 3 makes about Maya. (A) reverses main and secondary: honoring dispatchers is the occasion, and the bill is where the argument leads. (B) inflates one paragraph into the essay's purpose; Maya's story shows what dispatchers do (paragraph 3) and why the writer stays (paragraph 7). (D) misreads paragraph 2, where the writer says the public's not thinking about dispatchers 'is how it should be,' which is not a complaint.
parts.n: RHS-1.C (a text may have more than one purpose), skill 1.A. Thinking: explain how a secondary purpose serves the primary one instead of listing them. Trap: (A), which mistakes the occasion for the purpose.

parts.q:
In paragraph 2, the writer notes that this is 'the one week a year when cities print proclamations about people like me.' Which best describes how she uses this occasion?
(A) She accepts the week's praise with gratitude, which prepares for the thanks that she offers her readers in the essay's final paragraph.
(B) She uses the attention the week brings to argue that praise matters less than a change in the way the state classifies dispatchers.
(C) She dismisses the week's proclamations as meaningless, a choice that risks offending readers who value civic ceremonies.
(D) She uses the week to explain why the public has not thought about dispatchers until now, which is the main point of her essay.
parts.a: (B). The writer turns the occasion toward her argument: the week's attention is her opening ('I would like to use it to tell you what the proclamations leave out'), and she returns to it twice, telling readers they 'do not need to send a card' but should call about the bill, and ending 'The proclamations are nice. The drawing is why I stay.' The occasion gives her an audience, and she spends that attention on classification, pay, and retention. (A) finds thanks that is not there; paragraph 7 contrasts the proclamations with the drawing and thanks no one. (C) overstates her attitude: 'The proclamations are nice' grants their value while insisting they are not enough. (D) confuses a passing explanation with the point: why the public overlooks dispatchers takes two sentences, and it does not depend on the week at all.
parts.n: RHS-1.E (context: time, place and occasion), skill 1.A. Thinking: explain how a writer repurposes a ceremonial occasion for an argument. Trap: (C), which hears the writer's reservation about the proclamations as contempt.

parts.q:
In paragraph 3, the writer sets a paramedic's phrase, 'the first first responders,' against the state's listing of dispatchers 'alongside the people who file permits at the county courthouse.' Why is this contrast likely to persuade newspaper readers?
(A) Readers have just watched her guide a child through CPR, so they can judge for themselves how poorly the listing fits the work.
(B) Readers are likely to share the writer's low opinion of clerical work, so the listing will strike them as an insult to dispatchers.
(C) Readers will recognize the paramedic's phrase as the official term that settles how dispatchers must be classified by the state.
(D) Readers learn from the contrast that the writer respects clerical workers and would like to see them reclassified as well.
parts.a: (A). The contrast comes right after the account of Maya's call, so readers do not have to take the writer's word that the listing is wrong: they have just seen the work, and they can measure it against 'file permits' themselves. A comparison persuades when the audience already holds the knowledge it depends on, and the essay has supplied that knowledge a paragraph earlier. (B) misreads the writer's attitude; nothing in the essay disparages permit clerks, and a comparison that depended on contempt would put off readers who do such work. The contrast shows a mismatch, not a ranking. (C) turns a colleague's remark into a legal term; 'in the words of a paramedic I work with' marks it as informal testimony. (D) goes beyond the essay, which argues only about dispatchers and proposes nothing for other clerical jobs.
parts.n: RHS-1.K (a comparison works when the audience shares what it relies on), skill 1.B. Thinking: explain why a contrast lands with readers because of what the essay placed just before it. Trap: (B), which reads the contrast as a sneer at clerical work.

parts.q:
Which of the following additions would most directly strengthen the writer's claim in paragraph 5 that the city is 'already paying for the turnover'?
(A) The number of dispatchers who have left the center in each of the last five years, set out year by year
(B) A statement from a legislator who supports House Bill 212 and has promised to vote for it this month
(C) A description of the weeks of training that a new dispatcher must complete before taking calls alone
(D) An estimate of the bill's yearly cost to the city beside the yearly cost of replacing those who leave
parts.a: (D). The claim is a comparison: the money the bill would cost is money the city already spends, only 'after the fact.' The claim can be tested only by setting the two yearly costs side by side, and if replacement costs come close to the bill's cost, the legislators' objection loses most of its force. (A) is half right: a pattern of departures shows the turnover is persistent, but without the bill's cost it cannot show the city is already paying as much. (B) adds an endorsement, which speaks to the bill's support, not to the arithmetic of its cost. (C) would explain why training is expensive, but, again, nothing is set against the bill's price, so the comparison the claim depends on is still missing.
parts.n: RHS-1.H (a logical appeal needs evidence that fits its claim), skill 1.B. Thinking: identify what the claim compares, then choose the evidence that would test that comparison. Trap: (A), relevant to turnover but not to the cost comparison.

parts.q:
In paragraph 2, the writer tells readers, 'You have probably never thought about me, which is how it should be.' What does she imply by this remark?
(A) Readers who have never needed a dispatcher have been fortunate, so not knowing about her work is no fault of theirs.
(B) Dispatchers prefer to go unrecognized by the public and find the week's proclamations about their work embarrassing.
(C) The public has no reason to concern itself with how the city's emergency services are staffed or funded each year.
(D) She resents readers for failing to appreciate her work until something in their own lives has gone badly wrong.
parts.a: (A). The next sentence explains the remark: 'Nobody thinks about the dispatcher unless something has gone wrong, and on most days, for most of you, nothing has.' Not thinking about her is a sign of good fortune. By excusing the readers' ignorance instead of scolding it, the writer avoids blaming the very people she will ask, in paragraph 6, to call their representatives. (B) contradicts the essay: she calls the proclamations 'nice' and uses the week for her argument. (C) contradicts her purpose; the essay asks readers to act on how dispatchers are classified and staffed. (D) reverses the tone: she presents their not knowing as fortune, not as a failure to appreciate her.
parts.n: RHS-1.G (relating to an audience's values without alienating it), skill 1.B. Thinking: infer the attitude behind a remark from the sentence that follows it, and see what it does for the later request. Trap: (D), which hears resentment in what is framed as good luck.

parts.q:
A student suggests that the essay would be more persuasive if it ended with paragraph 6, so that readers finished on the request to call their representatives. Which of the following best evaluates the suggestion?
(A) It is sound, because an argument should end on its most important request, and the story of the drawing pulls attention away from the bill itself.
(B) It is sound, because the sentimental tone of paragraph 7 undercuts the figures on turnover and on training costs in paragraphs 4 and 5.
(C) It is unsound, because paragraph 7 completes the opening story and ends on why a dispatcher stays, which gives readers a reason to keep them.
(D) It is unsound, because the drawing is the essay's strongest evidence that dispatchers should be reclassified as first responders.
parts.a: (C). The essay's problem is dispatchers leaving (paragraph 4), and its last line answers with what keeps one of them: 'The drawing is why I stay.' Paragraph 7 also resolves the suspense of paragraph 1 (Maya's father lived), so the essay closes the frame it opened and leaves readers with an image of what is lost when a dispatcher quits. That gives the request in paragraph 6 a human stake. (A) states a rule about conclusions that does not hold; an ending may connect to the introduction or leave a compelling image rather than repeat a request. (B) treats emotion as a weakness in itself; the figures establish the problem and the drawing makes readers care about it, and the two work together. (D) overstates what the drawing shows: it explains why she stays, not how the state should classify her work, an argument that rests on paragraph 3.
parts.n: RHS-1.J (what a conclusion does beyond a call to act), skill 1.A. Thinking: judge a proposed cut by what the final paragraph adds to the argument and to the frame. Trap: (A), a rule that the final word must be the request.

mc.stem:
Questions 20-25 refer to the following.

The following passage is a draft of a letter that a high school junior is writing to the five members of her town's historic preservation commission, which must approve any change to the outside of a building in the town's historic district. The commission's members are an architect, two local historians, and two longtime owners of downtown buildings. (Written for practice; the writer, the town, and the commission are invented.)

(1) My name is Lena Ortiz, and I am a junior at Harwood High School. (2) I am writing to ask the commission to approve a mural on the east wall of the Kessler Feed Mill on Front Street. (3) The mural would show the mill as it looked in 1908, when farm wagons lined up along Front Street to have their grain ground. (4) Right now that wall is a boring blank slab of brick that nobody bothers to look at.

(5) Our school's art club has spent four months researching the design, working from photographs at the county historical society. (6) Some people may feel that a mural does not belong in a historic district. (7) But the commission already protects the faded advertisement for Kessler's Best Flour that was painted on the mill's north wall in the 1920s. (8) We would use mineral paint, which bonds with brick without trapping moisture inside it. (9) Mrs. Ruth Kessler Dunn, the granddaughter of the mill's founder, owns the building and has given us written permission. (10) Also, murals are really popular right now, and lots of towns have them.

(11) Honestly, some of the commission's rules seem kind of old-fashioned, but I hope you will make an exception this time. (12) Thank you for reading my letter.

parts.q:
In sentence 4 (reproduced below), the writer wants to describe the east wall in a way that will not offend readers who care about old buildings, while still showing why the wall suits a mural.
'Right now that wall is a boring blank slab of brick that nobody bothers to look at.'
Which version of sentence 4 best achieves this goal?
(A) Right now that wall is a wide expanse of aging brick that does little for the look of Front Street.
(B) Right now that wall is completely blank, which wastes one of the best locations downtown.
(C) Right now that wall is a plain face of brick, just as it has been for more than a hundred years.
(D) Right now that wall, unlike the north wall, carries no trace of the work the mill once did.
parts.a: (D). The revision describes the blank wall in the commission's own terms, history, so the mural becomes a way to restore a record of the mill's working life rather than to decorate a dull surface. It also prepares for the comparison with the north wall's flour advertisement in sentence 7. (A) softens the insult but still treats old brick as a blemish; 'aging' and 'does little for the look' disparage exactly what these readers protect. (B) removes the insult but judges the wall by its value as a location, which is the writer's interest, not the commission's. (C) is respectful but works against the request: a wall unchanged for a century sounds like part of the historic fabric the commission should leave alone.
parts.n: RHS-1.M (word choice reveals bias and affects credibility), skill 2.B. Thinking: find the wording that keeps the writer's point while speaking from the audience's values. Trap: (C), polite in tone but an argument for leaving the wall as it is.

parts.q:
The writer wants to replace sentence 10 with evidence that is most likely to persuade this commission to approve the mural. Which of the following best achieves this goal?
(A) A survey in which most students at Harwood High School said that they would like to see more public art in the downtown area
(B) The case of a nearby town whose preservation board approved a mineral-paint mural on a historic bank, with no damage to the brick years later
(C) A quotation from a nationally known muralist about the power of public art to bring the members of a community together
(D) Figures from a state tourism study showing that towns with downtown murals draw more weekend visitors than towns without them
parts.a: (B). A preservation commission must ask two questions about any change: whether a body like itself has allowed such a change, and whether the change harms the historic material. A comparable board's approval, followed by years without damage, answers both, and it supports sentence 8's claim about mineral paint with a result. (A) shows student support, which a commission charged with protecting buildings has little reason to weigh. (C) is an appeal to an authority from outside preservation, and it speaks to the benefits of art, not to the building's safety. (D) is the strongest distractor, since the two building owners may care about visitors, but it does not address the commission's duty and could even raise the worry that the district will be turned into an attraction.
parts.n: RHS-1.N (choosing evidence for this audience's needs), skill 2.B. Thinking: identify what this audience must decide, then choose the evidence that addresses it. Trap: (D), strong evidence for a different audience, such as a chamber of commerce.

parts.q:
The writer is considering deleting sentence 11. Should she make this deletion?
(A) Yes, because the sentence belittles the rules that the readers are responsible for upholding and asks them to set those rules aside.
(B) Yes, because the sentence only repeats the request stated in sentence 2 and adds no new information that the commission needs.
(C) No, because the sentence shows the writer's honesty about her own views, and that honesty will strengthen her credibility.
(D) No, because the sentence acknowledges the objection raised in sentence 6 and shows the writer understands the commission's concerns.
parts.a: (A). The commission's members wrote or enforce the rules that sentence 11 calls 'kind of old-fashioned,' and the casual 'Honestly' and 'kind of' make the dismissal sound careless. Worse, 'make an exception' concedes that the mural breaks the rules, which undercuts the argument of sentences 7 and 8 that the mural fits what the commission already protects. (B) reaches the right decision for the wrong reason: the problem with sentence 11 is not repetition but the attitude it reveals toward the readers. (C) confuses candor with credibility; a writer who disparages the audience's values loses standing with it, however honest she is. (D) misreads the sentence: it does not acknowledge the objection in sentence 6, it dismisses the commission's rules.
parts.n: RHS-1.L (diction and syntax shape how the audience perceives the writer), skill 2.B. Thinking: judge a sentence by how it positions the writer against the readers' values and her own argument. Trap: (B), the right decision with a reason that misses the real problem.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add a sentence before sentence 1 that will engage this particular audience before she introduces herself and states her request. Which of the following best achieves this goal?
(A) Public art has been a part of human culture ever since people first painted animals on the walls of caves.
(B) Have you ever walked down Front Street and wished that its old brick buildings had a little more color?
(C) In the fall of 1908, as many as forty farm wagons a day lined up along Front Street to reach the Kessler mill.
(D) Studies show that students who work on community art projects are more likely to take part in civic life.
parts.a: (C). A historical scene, specific to Front Street and to this building, speaks to readers who include two local historians and whose job is to protect the district's past. It also previews the mural's subject (sentence 3), so the request arrives as a way to bring that scene back. (A) is a sweeping generalization that says nothing about Harwood, the mill, or preservation. (B) engages the reader with a question, but its premise, that the historic district needs 'more color,' is the one most likely to put this commission on guard. (D) addresses what the project does for students, which is not the question the commission must decide.
parts.n: RHS-1.I (an introduction that orients and engages a particular audience), skill 2.A. Thinking: choose the opening strategy whose content fits these readers' interests, not just an engaging form. Trap: (B), an engaging question built on a premise this audience rejects.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that makes the comparison between the mural and the old flour advertisement more persuasive to the commission. Which of the following best achieves this goal?
(A) Both are paintings on the outside walls of the mill, and both can be seen clearly by people walking along Front Street.
(B) Unlike that faded advertisement, which is now hard to read, the mural would be bright and easy to see from the street.
(C) The advertisement proves that the commission has approved paintings on historic buildings and should do so again.
(D) Like that advertisement, the mural would record a piece of the mill's working life on the building where it happened.
parts.a: (D). A comparison persuades when it rests on a likeness the audience already values. The commission protects the flour advertisement because it records the mill's history in the place where that history happened; the added sentence claims the same value for the mural. (A) rests on a surface likeness, paint on a wall, which a preservation commission would not find decisive. (B) turns the comparison against the writer: brightness and newness are exactly what separate a mural from a historic sign, which the commission values because it is old. (C) overclaims: protecting an old sign is not the same as approving a new painting, and 'should do so again' asserts the conclusion instead of supporting it.
parts.n: RHS-1.K (a comparison must rest on something the audience shares), skill 2.B. Thinking: find the ground of likeness that matters to this audience, not any likeness at all. Trap: (C), which treats the comparison as a precedent it does not establish.

parts.q:
The writer wants to replace sentence 12 with a conclusion that asks the commission for a specific action and connects to the beginning of the letter. Which of the following best achieves this goal?
(A) Thank you for your time, and I hope that you will give my request the careful consideration that it deserves.
(B) Public art makes a town a better place to live, and I hope that Harwood will not be left behind other towns.
(C) I hope you will approve the mural at your May 6 meeting, so that the wagons of 1908 can line up on Front Street again.
(D) If you have any questions about the mural, please contact me or our art club's adviser at Harwood High School.
parts.a: (C). The sentence asks for the commission's vote at a named meeting and returns to the image of sentence 3, the wagons lined up along Front Street in 1908, so the letter ends where it began and in the commission's own terms. (A) is polite but asks for no specific action and connects to nothing earlier. (B) reaches for broader significance but names no action and presents approval as a race with other towns, which echoes sentence 10, the draft's weakest argument. (D) names a specific action, but a minor one (asking questions) rather than the approval, and it does not connect to the letter's beginning.
parts.n: RHS-1.J (a conclusion that calls to action and connects to the introduction), skill 2.A. Thinking: test each choice against both halves of the stated goal. Trap: (D), which meets the first half of the goal and not the second.

fr.title: Rhetorical analysis: a publisher's last-chance letter to her town
fr.stem:
In 2025, the Cold Spring Ledger, a weekly newspaper that had been published in a small river town for 112 years, printed the following letter from its publisher on its front page. Over the previous ten years the paper had lost nearly half of its subscribers. (The newspaper, the town, and the publisher are invented for practice.)

Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the publisher makes to persuade her readers to subscribe.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
• Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

To the people of Cold Spring:

For 112 years, this newspaper has told you who was born, who married, who died, and what the town council did on Tuesday night. Today I have to tell you something about the Ledger itself, and I would rather you heard it from me than from a rumor at the diner.

Unless 600 more of you subscribe by the last day of this month, the issue of October 30 will be our last.

I will not dress that number up. The Ledger has 1,340 subscribers today; ten years ago it had 2,500. Advertising has fallen even faster, and the plant that prints us raised its price again in June. I have cut my own salary twice, and I have cut the paper from twenty pages to twelve. There is nothing left to cut but the paper itself.

You may be thinking that you get your news on your phone now, and many of you do. But ask where that news comes from. When the county tried to close the Route 9 bridge last spring without a hearing, the story that forced the hearing ran on this page, after our reporter, Dan Iverson, sat through four hours of a meeting nobody else attended. When the school budget came up two million dollars short, it was the Ledger that read all 214 pages of it. Your phone did not send anyone to those meetings. It passed along what we wrote.

A town without a newspaper does not go quiet. It fills up with guesses. Every rumor about the bridge, the school, or the new warehouse out on Quarry Road will travel just as fast as it does now, and there will be no one whose job it is to check.

A subscription costs 52 dollars a year, a dollar a week, less than a cup of coffee at the diner. I know a dollar is not nothing to everyone in this town. If it is too much for you, call me. I have never turned away a reader who asked, and I will not start now.

But if you have been meaning to subscribe, or you let your subscription lapse, or you read your neighbor's copy on the porch every Thursday, this is the month.

I would like to write the October 30 issue about something else.

Margaret Holloway, Publisher

rows.earns: A defensible thesis that analyzes the publisher's choices in light of her purpose and audience, for example: 'Writing to neighbors who have drifted to their phones, Holloway earns their trust with blunt numbers about the paper's decline, then shows them, through the bridge and the school budget, that the news they already read depends on the Ledger, so that subscribing feels less like charity to a failing business than like paying for something the town already uses.' The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear in the introduction or the conclusion.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('Holloway uses rhetorical choices to persuade readers to subscribe'); naming appeals with no link to purpose ('she uses ethos, pathos, and logos'); summarizing the letter; or a thesis about newspapers in general ('local news is important') rather than about her choices.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence from the letter supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how each choice works on these readers. Strong essays explain, for example, how the opening list ('who was born, who married, who died') reminds readers of the paper's place in their own lives before any request; how the bare deadline set off in its own paragraph and the refusal to 'dress that number up' build credibility with readers who might suspect a sales pitch; how the cuts to her own salary show that she has shared the loss before asking anyone else to; how the anticipated objection ('you get your news on your phone') is turned, through the Route 9 bridge and the 214-page budget, into evidence that the phone depends on the paper; how 'does not go quiet. It fills up with guesses' makes the loss concrete for a town that already trades rumors 'at the diner'; how the dollar-a-week comparison and the offer to readers who cannot pay address the audience's different means; and how the understated last line leaves readers to imagine the story of the paper's closing.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence for each claim, but commentary explains only some of it, or explains choices without tying them to these readers. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates or paraphrases the letter ('she says the paper might close, which is sad'), or labels appeals without explaining their effect. 1: summary with little analysis, or evidence that is mostly general. 0: restates the thesis or is irrelevant. Three paragraphs on 'ethos,' 'pathos,' and 'logos' that each quote a line and name the appeal, with no account of what the choice does for this audience, cannot score above 2.

rows.earns: Explaining the significance or complexity of the rhetorical situation, for example that Holloway must ask for money without sounding like a business pleading for customers, and that her candor about the finances, her offer of free copies, and the neighbor's copy 'on the porch' all present the Ledger as a shared town institution rather than a product; or that the letter's own form, a front-page story about the paper, demonstrates the claim that without the Ledger no one would report such news; or a consistently vivid and persuasive style.
rows.loses: A single remark such as 'this letter shows the importance of local news today' added to the conclusion; listing many choices without a unifying explanation; or a sweeping claim about the internet and democracy that the essay does not develop.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that analyzes how the publisher's choices serve her purpose with these readers.
parts.a: Model: 'Holloway knows her readers are neighbors, not customers, and that many of them think they no longer need a newspaper; so she tells them the plain numbers first, which earns their trust, and then shows that the news on their phones comes from the Ledger's reporters, so that letting the paper close becomes a loss to the town rather than the failure of a business.' It names the audience's belief she must overcome, two strategies, and the purpose they serve.
parts.n: 'Holloway uses many rhetorical strategies, such as statistics and emotional language, to persuade her audience' names devices without saying what they do for these readers, and does not earn the point.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs in a line of reasoning, each with specific evidence and the commentary that explains how the choice works on these readers.
parts.a:
¶1 Candor as credibility: 'I would rather you heard it from me than from a rumor at the diner'; the deadline set alone in its own paragraph; 'I will not dress that number up'; the salary cut twice. Commentary: readers asked for money expect a pitch, and Holloway gives them a balance sheet instead, including her own sacrifice, so the request comes from someone who has already paid.
¶2 Turning the objection: 'you get your news on your phone now'; the Route 9 bridge, Dan Iverson's four hours, the 214 pages. Commentary: she grants the readers' habit instead of scolding it, then traces the phone's news back to her reporters; 'Your phone did not send anyone' converts the reason people stopped subscribing into the reason to start again.
¶3 Making the loss concrete, and the request possible for everyone: 'does not go quiet. It fills up with guesses'; 'a dollar a week'; 'If it is too much for you, call me'; the neighbor's copy on the porch. Commentary: she pictures the town after the paper, full of unchecked rumors, and then lowers every barrier to acting, addressing readers of different means, lapsed readers, and even the ones reading for free. The last line, 'I would like to write the October 30 issue about something else,' leaves the readers to supply the headline they would be responsible for.
parts.n: A plan that lists 'ethos: salary cut; pathos: rumors; logos: 1,340 subscribers' with no commentary on these readers earns at most 2; each paragraph needs a claim about what the choice does for this audience.

parts.q: Row C plan: explain how this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Carry one tension through the essay: Holloway must ask for money while insisting that the Ledger is not merely selling something. Each paragraph shows how a choice resolves that tension, from the salary cuts (she shares the loss) to the offer of free subscriptions (the paper serves readers who cannot pay) to the final line (the town's story, not the company's). The conclusion can then note that the letter is itself an act of the reporting it defends: without a newspaper, no one would have told the town this story either.
parts.n: Ending with 'In today's world, local newspapers are disappearing everywhere' gestures at a broader context without explaining how it bears on Holloway's choices, and earns nothing.

fr.title: Audience and credibility: the superintendent's remarks in Marlow
fr.stem:
The paragraphs below are from the superintendent's remarks to Marlow parents in questions 1-7. Reread them and answer the questions that follow. (Written for practice; the speaker, the district, and the places are invented.)

[2] Some of you know that I went to a school like this one. It had four classrooms, a gravel lot, and a principal who knew which of us had a sick grandmother and which of us had not eaten breakfast. It closed when I was nine. I remember the bus ride to the new school, and I remember that for most of that first year nobody there knew my name. I tell you this not to ask for your sympathy but because it tells me exactly what I owe your children: that no child from Marlow will spend a year at Carver Street being a stranger.

[4] I know what some of you are thinking, because several of you have told me: that this is how it always goes, that the county seat takes and the villages give. I will not pretend that fear comes from nowhere. The post office went, and then the bank branch. But a school is not a bank branch. A school is where a village sees its own children every morning, and when it goes, something goes with it that no budget line records.

[5] But I would ask you to consider what the board was weighing. Twelve years ago Marlow Elementary enrolled 212 students; this year it enrolled 71. Its third grade had six children in it. Its roof needs a repair estimated at 1.4 million dollars, more than the district spends on textbooks in five years. The board did not choose between a good school and a bad one. It chose between two ways of losing something, and it chose the one it believed would cost your children less.

parts.q: Paragraph 4 states the parents' fear in terms at least as strong as they might use themselves, and paragraph 5 then gives the board's figures. Explain how placing paragraph 4 before paragraph 5 is likely to affect the way this audience receives the figures.
parts.a: Because the speaker first grants the full weight of the loss, even saying that it is something 'no budget line records,' the parents cannot easily hear the figures in paragraph 5 as the view of an official who thinks the school is only a budget line. He has shown that he sees what they value, so 'I would ask you to consider what the board was weighing' reads as a request to look at the other side of a scale he has admitted is heavy, not as a dismissal. Had the enrollment and roof figures come first, a distrustful audience would likely have taken them as proof of the indifference paragraph 4 describes, and stopped listening before the concession.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'paragraph 4 uses pathos and paragraph 5 uses logos' or 'it makes the speech more organized,' neither of which explains how the order changes the way these listeners hear the numbers.

parts.q: A student argues: 'The superintendent's story in paragraph 2 is manipulative. He uses a painful childhood memory to get the parents to stop objecting to a decision he supports.' Evaluate the student's argument, using evidence from the passage.
parts.a: The argument is only partly right. The story does carry emotion, and placed early it builds goodwill before the figures in paragraph 5. But it is not used to end the parents' objections; it binds the speaker to a standard they can hold him to: 'it tells me exactly what I owe your children: that no child from Marlow will spend a year at Carver Street being a stranger.' The speech then invites continued scrutiny rather than silence, with commitments in writing and a council that can tell the district 'in public, when we fall short.' Manipulation would use emotion to move the audience against its own interests; here the emotion commits the speaker to the children's interests, so the story is better described as a pledge than as a tactic.
parts.n: Earns nothing: agreeing because 'any emotional appeal is manipulation'; or disagreeing only because 'the story is true,' since the question is what the story does in the speech, not whether it happened.

parts.q: The superintendent will give a shorter version of these remarks to parents at Carver Street Elementary, the school that will receive the Marlow children. Name one choice from the Marlow remarks that he should change for that audience and one that he should keep, and justify each by explaining what the Carver Street parents are likely to believe or need.
parts.a: Change paragraph 4: it answers a fear, losing the village school, that Carver Street parents do not have. Their likelier worries are crowding, larger classes, and stretched resources, so he should replace it with what answers those, for example that the six Marlow teachers are moving with the children, so class sizes need not rise. Keep the story in paragraph 2, turned toward the new audience: 'nobody there knew my name' becomes a request to the receiving school's families, who can make sure the Marlow children are not strangers. (Keeping the written, checkable commitments of paragraph 3 is also defensible: any audience facing a change it did not choose trusts promises it can verify.) The point requires both a change and a keep, and each must be justified by a belief or need of the Carver Street parents; either defensible keep (paragraph 2 or paragraph 3) qualifies.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'he should use more logos' or 'he should keep the emotional parts' without naming what the Carver Street parents believe or need; or a change that ignores the new audience, such as cutting the figures 'because they are sad.'

fr.title: Writing for the room: recruiting reading volunteers at a senior center
fr.stem:
A high school senior who helps run a reading program at Lincoln Elementary School has been invited to speak for five minutes at the monthly luncheon of the Riverside Senior Center, whose members are mostly retired residents of the town. She hopes to recruit volunteers to read with second graders one hour a week. Below is the opening of her draft. The sentences are numbered. (Written for practice; the student, the school, and the center are invented.)

(1) Hi everyone, and thanks for having me! (2) I know that a lot of you are retired and have tons of free time, so I figured this would be a great fit. (3) Lincoln Elementary needs reading volunteers, and the district's latest data show that only 58 percent of our second graders are meeting their benchmark Lexile targets. (4) You don't need any special training, and we'll even show you how to use the reading app on our tablets. (5) So please sign up!

parts.q: Choose one word or phrase in sentences 2 through 4 that is likely to lower the speaker's credibility with this audience. Explain why, with reference to what these listeners are likely to believe or value.
parts.a: 'Tons of free time' (sentence 2) assumes that retirement means idleness. Many of these listeners care for grandchildren, volunteer elsewhere, or manage their health, and would hear the phrase as dismissive; it also frames the request as filling their empty hours rather than as needing what they know, which tells them the speaker has not thought about who they are. Other choices can earn the point with the same kind of reasoning: 'benchmark Lexile targets' is school jargon that treats the listeners as outsiders, and 'we'll even show you how to use the reading app' implies, through 'even,' that they would struggle with a tablet.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the tone is too casual' without naming a phrase and explaining what this audience believes; or naming a phrase with no account of how these listeners would hear it.

parts.q: Rewrite sentences 1 and 2 so that they relate the request to a value this audience is likely to hold. Then explain in one sentence why you chose that value.
parts.a: Model: 'Many of you learned to read at a kitchen table, next to someone who had the patience to wait while you sounded out a word. The second graders at Lincoln Elementary need that same patience, and I am here to ask whether some of you would give them one hour a week.' Why: it appeals to the listeners' own memories and to the value of passing on what someone once gave them, so they are asked for their experience and patience, not their spare time.
parts.n: Earns nothing: a rewrite that only removes the slang ('Good afternoon. Since many of you are retired and have free time...') and keeps the same assumption; or a rewrite with no value named or explained.

parts.q: The student has time for only one piece of evidence. She is choosing between (i) the district's figure that 58 percent of second graders meet the reading benchmark and (ii) a statement from a retired machinist who volunteered last year: 'I thought I was going there to help a kid read. By March he was reading me the sports page.' Which should she use with this audience? Justify your choice, and explain what the other option would lose or risk.
parts.a: The machinist's statement. A retired listener's likeliest unspoken question is whether someone like me can do this, and whether it will matter; a peer's words answer both, and 'reading me the sports page' shows progress in a form they can picture. The statistic establishes the need, but in the district's terms: a bare percentage does not tell a retiree what one hour of their time achieves, and it risks sounding like the school's problem rather than a child's. Choosing the statistic can also earn the point if the answer justifies it with this audience's needs, for example by translating it into 'about four in ten second graders are behind' to show the scale that a single story cannot.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the statistic, because numbers are more convincing' or 'the quotation, because it uses pathos,' with no reference to what this audience needs; or a choice that never says what the other option would lose.
