mc.stem:
Questions 1-7 refer to the following.

The following passage is a column published in a city newspaper shortly after the school district adopted a pacing calendar, which sets the date by which every class must finish each unit. The sentences are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer, the newspaper, and the district are invented.)

(1) The district's new pacing calendar has been called rigid, and I would like to defend it by pointing out that it does not go nearly far enough. (2) The calendar tells each teacher which unit to finish by which Friday; it does not yet address the chief obstacle to finishing anything on time, which is the student who raises a hand.

(3) Consider the costs. (4) A single question from a single ninth grader ("Wait, why does that work?") can consume four minutes of instruction, and four minutes, multiplied across thirty students and a hundred and eighty days, is a loss no calendar can absorb. (5) Worse, questions are contagious. (6) One student asks why; a second, emboldened, asks what would happen if; by the third question, the class has wandered entirely off the calendar and into the subject.

(7) I therefore propose a modest fee: a nickel per question, payable in advance. (8) The fee would be low enough that no child is prevented from asking and high enough that every child would think twice, which is, after all, what we have always wanted children to do. (9) Questions about logistics ("Which page?") would be free. (10) Questions beginning with "why" would cost a dime, since they so rarely have short answers, and questions beginning with "what if" would be banned outright, as not one of them has ever been answered within a single class period.

(11) The benefits are easy to picture. (12) Lessons would end on the minute. (13) Units would close on their assigned Fridays. (14) Teachers, relieved of the burden of discovering what their students do not understand, could devote themselves entirely to the calendar. (15) And students would learn a valuable lesson about the cost of time, if about nothing else.

(16) I recognize that some parents will object to charging children for their curiosity. (17) To them I say only that the calendar is already charging it. (18) Every teacher in this district now knows exactly how many days she has left for fractions, and every teacher now has to decide, each time a hand goes up, whether the question in it is worth falling behind. (19) My fee is a nickel. (20) The calendar's fee is the question itself, and it is paid by the child who, having learned what questions cost, stops asking them.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the writer's actual position?
(A) The writer supports the calendar and wants it strengthened with a fee that would keep every class on schedule.
(B) The writer opposes the calendar, because by penalizing delay it discourages the questions through which students learn.
(C) The writer accepts the calendar but opposes the fee, which would fall hardest on families who could not afford it.
(D) The writer has no settled view of the calendar and asks parents to weigh its costs and benefits for themselves.
parts.a: (B). The proposal is ironic: the writer 'defends' the calendar by pushing its logic to an absurd fee, and sentences 17-20 drop the pose to say what the writer objects to. The calendar already makes teachers weigh each question against falling behind, and its cost is 'paid by the child who... stops asking.' (A) takes the proposal at face value and misses its cues, such as the ban on 'what if' questions and sentence 15's 'if about nothing else.' (C) treats the fee as a real proposal the writer might oppose, but the writer invented the fee, and the only thing sentences 16-20 criticize is the calendar. (D) mistakes the column's indirection for neutrality; sentence 20 states a clear judgment.
parts.n: STL-1.R (irony emerges from the gap between an argument and readers' values), skill 7.A. Thinking: infer a writer's real position from an ironic surface and the point where the irony drops. Trap: (C), which half-sees the irony but still treats the fee as the thing under debate.

parts.q:
In sentence 6, placing the phrase 'and into the subject' at the very end of the sentence chiefly serves to
(A) show that the writer regards students' questions as a distraction from the unit that the class is supposed to be covering
(B) complete the series of questions begun earlier in the sentence, so that the three students' questions are balanced
(C) signal a shift from the ironic tone of the column to the plain, sincere tone of the column's final paragraph
(D) reveal, in the sentence's last words, that what the calendar treats as a detour is the learning itself
parts.a: (D). The sentence builds as if describing a class losing its way ('wandered entirely off the calendar') and then ends where a reader expects a word like 'off topic' with 'into the subject.' The final position gives the twist its force: questions lead students into the subject the calendar is supposed to serve. (A) reads the sentence literally, as the column's pretended voice would; the end placement undercuts that view. (B) misdescribes the structure: the series of students ends with 'by the third question,' and the final phrase is not a fourth item but the turn. (C) misplaces the shift, which comes in sentence 17; sentence 6 is still in the ironic voice, and the joke works inside it.
parts.n: STL-1.L (the arrangement of words in a sentence can emphasize ideas), skill 7.B. Thinking: explain what the end position of a phrase does to the meaning of the whole sentence. Trap: (A), the literal reading the irony is built to overturn.

parts.q:
In sentence 14, the phrase 'relieved of the burden of discovering what their students do not understand' contributes to the column's irony chiefly by
(A) suggesting that teachers already find the work of discovering what students do not understand a tiresome chore
(B) using technical terms from education research that the newspaper's general readers would not recognize
(C) describing the center of a teacher's work in words usually reserved for a hardship someone is glad to escape
(D) conceding that the calendar would give teachers more time, a benefit the writer takes seriously in sentence 18
parts.a: (C). 'Relieved of the burden' is the language of rescue from a hardship. Attaching it to 'discovering what their students do not understand,' which is what teaching is, exposes the proposal's values: a calendar that frees teachers from teaching. (A) attributes the pretended attitude to teachers; nothing in the column says they find the work tiresome, and the irony depends on readers knowing they do not. (B) mistakes plain words for jargon; the phrase is ordinary, which is why the mismatch is easy to hear. (D) misreads sentence 18, which says teachers must now weigh each question against falling behind; that is a cost, not a benefit.
parts.n: STL-1.A (connotation), with STL-1.R, skill 7.A. Thinking: explain how the connotation of a phrase clashes with what it describes. Trap: (A), which assigns the column's pretended attitude to the people it describes.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the change in tone that begins in sentence 17?
(A) From mock-earnest to plainly serious, as the writer drops the pretense of the proposal and names what the calendar costs
(B) From amused to bitter, as the writer gives up on persuading readers and turns instead to criticizing the district's teachers
(C) From sincere to sarcastic, as the writer abandons a practical proposal and begins to mock the parents who object to it
(D) From confident to uncertain, as the writer admits that the proposed fee might cost students more than the calendar does
parts.a: (A). Through sentence 16 the writer speaks as a straight-faced advocate of the fee. Sentence 17 ('the calendar is already charging it') drops the pose, and sentences 18-20 speak plainly about teachers weighing each raised hand and the child who 'stops asking.' The shift reveals the column's real target. (B) misreads the teachers in sentence 18 as the target; the writer presents them as constrained by the calendar, not at fault. (C) reverses the direction: the column moves from ironic to sincere, and the parents of sentence 16 are answered, not mocked. (D) inverts sentences 19-20, which set a trivial nickel against the calendar's far larger cost; the writer does not doubt which is greater.
parts.n: STL-1.F (a shift in tone can signal a qualification or reconsideration of perspective), skill 7.A. Thinking: name the direction of a tone shift and what it reveals about the writer's perspective. Trap: (C), which gets the direction of the shift backward.

parts.q:
A reader responds in a letter to the newspaper: 'Charging children a nickel to ask a question is cruel, and I am shocked that the paper printed this proposal.' Which of the following best evaluates the reader's response?
(A) The reader is right, since the writer admits in sentence 16 that parents will object to charging children for curiosity.
(B) The reader is wrong, since a nickel is small enough that, as sentence 8 says, no child would be prevented from asking.
(C) The reader takes the proposal literally, missing cues such as the ban on 'what if' and sentence 20's turn against the calendar.
(D) The reader's response is fair, since a satirical column is obliged to state its real position plainly in its very first sentence.
parts.a: (C). The column's exaggerations (a dime for 'why,' a ban on 'what if' because such questions are never answered in one period, students learning about time 'if about nothing else') signal that the proposal is not meant seriously, and sentences 17-20 say plainly that the cruelty the reader objects to is the calendar's. The reader shares the writer's values and has mistaken the target. (A) treats sentence 16 as an admission, but it sets up the reply that the calendar already charges the fee. (B) argues inside the ironic frame, defending a proposal the writer never meant. (D) states a rule satire does not follow; irony works by withholding the real position, and this column reveals it only at the end.
parts.n: STL-1.E (readers infer tone from word choice), with STL-1.R, skill 7.A. Thinking: judge a reader's response by the cues that should have signaled irony. Trap: (B), which answers the reader on the proposal's own terms.

parts.q:
The parallel clauses in sentence 8 ('low enough that no child is prevented from asking and high enough that every child would think twice') contribute to the column's irony chiefly by
(A) showing that the writer has weighed the interests of students and teachers and found them to be exactly equal
(B) giving the fee the balanced sound of a sensible compromise, which masks what the fee is designed to discourage
(C) placing more weight on the second clause than on the first, which reveals that the fee is meant to silence children
(D) introducing the list of free and costly questions in sentences 9-10, so that readers can see how the fee would work
parts.a: (B). The coordinated clauses 'low enough... and high enough' mimic the even-handed language of a policy compromise, so the fee sounds reasonable. Only the sentence's last clause, which treats 'think twice' (hesitate) as though it meant thinking, lets readers hear that the fee exists to make children hesitate to ask. (A) takes the balance as the writer's sincere judgment; the clauses weigh a child's asking against a child's hesitating, not students against teachers. (C) misreads coordination, which gives the two clauses equal weight; the irony comes from the balance, not from tipping it. (D) describes what follows the sentence, not what the parallel clauses themselves do.
parts.n: STL-1.J (coordination shows balance between ideas), skill 7.B. Thinking: explain how a balanced structure lends false reasonableness to an absurd idea. Trap: (C), which expects the second of two coordinate clauses to carry more weight.

parts.q:
A student argues that sentences 19 and 20 are unnecessary, since sentence 17 has already stated the writer's point. Which of the following best evaluates this argument?
(A) The student is right, since a column should end as soon as its central point has been stated, and sentence 17 states it.
(B) The student is right, since sentences 19-20 return to the ironic proposal after the column has begun to speak sincerely.
(C) The student is wrong, since sentences 19-20 offer the column's first evidence that the calendar has slowed classes down.
(D) The student is wrong, since sentences 19-20 set the pretend fee beside the real one and end by naming who pays it.
parts.a: (D). Sentence 17 asserts that the calendar 'is already charging it,' but only sentences 19-20 show what that charge is. The short sentence 'My fee is a nickel' sets up a contrast that the longer sentence 20 completes: the calendar's fee is 'the question itself,' paid by a child who stops asking. The arrangement puts the column's most important idea in its final words. (A) applies a rule of thumb that ignores what the last sentences add. (B) is half right, since sentence 19 recalls the proposal, but it does so only to measure it against the real cost, and the sentence is sincere. (C) misreads the sentences, which say nothing about pace; the calendar exists to keep classes on schedule, and the column's complaint is what that costs.
parts.n: STL-1.H (the arrangement of sentences can emphasize particular ideas), skill 7.B. Thinking: judge whether an ending adds to what came before, by what its arrangement emphasizes. Trap: (B), which notices the return to the nickel but not why it returns.

mc.stem:
Questions 8-13 refer to the following.

The two passages below concern the closing of a footbridge. Passage 1 is a statement posted on a city's website by its department of public works. Passage 2 is from a post on a neighborhood association's blog, written by a resident two days later. The sentences of each passage are numbered. (Written for practice; the city, the writers, and the bridge are invented.)

Passage 1

(1) The Mill Street Footbridge has been closed to all pedestrian and bicycle traffic, effective immediately, following the identification of a structural concern during a scheduled inspection on May 12. (2) Although minor surface cracking was noted during the 2023 inspection, the bridge remained within established safety guidelines until last week's findings. (3) The closure has been undertaken out of an abundance of caution. (4) Residents are advised to use the Elm Street Bridge (0.6 miles south) as an alternate route. (5) An engineering assessment is underway, and further information will be provided as it becomes available. (6) The Department appreciates the community's patience and remains committed to the safety of all residents.

Passage 2

(1) On Tuesday morning I walked my daughter to school the way we always go, across the Mill Street footbridge, and found it wrapped in orange fencing. (2) One sign said CLOSED. (3) Another said that the city apologized for any inconvenience. (4) The city's statement, posted that afternoon, says that a "structural concern" was "identified" on May 12. (5) I would like to identify it more precisely. (6) It is a crack in the concrete under the third lamppost, and it is not new. (7) I reported it to the city's hotline in April 2023, when it was as thin as a pencil line, and again last fall, when I could lay my daughter's school ruler in it (three-eighths of an inch, she informed me, with some pride). (8) Both times I received a polite email thanking me for my report.

(9) I am glad the bridge is closed. (10) I would rather walk the extra mile to Elm Street every morning than cross a bridge that is coming apart. (11) But I would like the city to stop describing its caution as abundant. (12) Abundant caution would have looked at the crack when a resident first pointed to it. (13) What the city showed was caution at the last possible moment, which is a different thing, and a smaller one.

parts.q:
In sentence 2 of Passage 1, placing the 2023 finding in a clause that begins with 'Although' has which of the following effects?
(A) It emphasizes the 2023 finding as the statement's most important fact, so that readers see how early the city was concerned.
(B) It gives the 2023 finding and the bridge's continued safety equal weight, so that readers can judge between the two of them.
(C) It presents the earlier cracking as a detail outweighed by the bridge's continued safety, not as an unheeded warning.
(D) It shows that the 2023 inspection was more thorough than last week's, since it found the cracking that the later one missed.
parts.a: (C). The 2023 finding sits in a subordinate clause ('Although minor surface cracking was noted...'), and the main clause carries the city's point: 'the bridge remained within established safety guidelines.' Subordination makes the earlier finding background, conceded and set aside, rather than a warning the city failed to act on, and 'minor' and 'surface' reinforce the effect. (A) reverses the emphasis, since a subordinate clause is the less emphatic position. (B) describes coordination, which would join the two ideas as equals with 'and' or 'but.' (D) invents a comparison between inspections; the statement says it was last week's inspection that found the structural concern.
parts.n: STL-1.K (subordination shows an imbalance between ideas), skill 7.B. Thinking: explain what a writer gains by putting an inconvenient fact in a subordinate clause. Trap: (A), which assumes a fact mentioned first must be the one emphasized.

parts.q:
Passage 1 refers to 'a structural concern' that was 'identified,' while Passage 2 refers to 'a crack in the concrete under the third lamppost.' This difference chiefly reflects
(A) Passage 2's more precise wording, which names the problem and its place and so makes it harder to treat as newly found
(B) Passage 1's greater technical accuracy, since an engineer's term is more exact than a resident's description of a crack
(C) Passage 2's informal style, which suits a blog but leaves its account of the bridge vaguer than the official statement
(D) Passage 1's wish to alarm residents, since vague language makes a danger sound larger than a specific description does
parts.a: (A). 'A crack in the concrete under the third lamppost' names what the problem is and where it is; 'a structural concern' names only a category. The precision serves Passage 2's purpose: a specific crack can be reported, measured, and dated ('as thin as a pencil line' in April 2023), so the city's 'identified' on May 12 no longer reads as a discovery. (B) confuses an abstract term with an exact one; 'structural concern' is the less precise of the two. (C) reverses the passages, since the blog gives the more specific account. (D) misreads Passage 1's purpose; its calm, abstract phrasing ('out of an abundance of caution') works to reassure, not to alarm.
parts.n: STL-1.C (precise word choice reduces confusion and conveys perspective), skill 7.A. Thinking: compare two descriptions of the same thing and explain what the more precise one lets its writer do. Trap: (B), which equates official-sounding language with accuracy.

parts.q:
In sentences 11-13 of Passage 2, the writer takes up the word 'abundant' from the city's phrase 'out of an abundance of caution' chiefly in order to
(A) agree that the city acted cautiously, while regretting the inconvenience that the closure has caused her family
(B) suggest that the city closed the bridge too hastily, before its engineering assessment could be completed
(C) mock the city's formal style in general, without disputing any of the facts that the city's statement reports
(D) turn the city's own word against it, arguing that caution which ignored two reports cannot be called abundant
parts.a: (D). Passage 1 says the closure was undertaken 'out of an abundance of caution.' Passage 2 takes up the word ('stop describing its caution as abundant') and measures it against her reports: abundant caution 'would have looked at the crack when a resident first pointed to it,' and what the city showed was 'caution at the last possible moment.' (A) is half right, since sentence 9 approves the closure, but the paragraph's point is to dispute the word, and sentence 10 accepts the inconvenience without complaint. (B) reverses the complaint: the writer thinks the city acted too late, not too soon. (C) misses that the writer disputes what the phrase implies, that the city's concern was prompt and generous.
parts.n: STL-1.E (readers infer tone from the connotations of words), skill 7.A. Thinking: infer the attitude a writer conveys by repeating an opponent's word in a new context. Trap: (A), which stops at sentence 9's approval of the closure.

parts.q:
Which of the following best evaluates how the style of Passage 1 serves the department's purpose, and what that style leaves out?
(A) Its technical vocabulary shows the engineers' expertise, though it leaves out how long the closure is likely to last.
(B) Its impersonal sentences, which seldom say who acted, report the closure while leaving aside who knew what, and when.
(C) Its warm, personal tone shows the department shares residents' frustration, though it omits how far the detour is.
(D) Its short, blunt sentences convey the danger's urgency, though they leave out what the 2023 inspection found.
parts.a: (B). Passage 1's verbs mostly omit the actor: the bridge 'has been closed,' cracking 'was noted,' the closure 'has been undertaken,' information 'will be provided.' That style gives residents what they need, the closure, the detour, and the promise of updates, while keeping out of view the question Passage 2 raises: who saw the cracking, and what was done about it. As a source, the statement shows what the city wants residents to know more than what happened. (A) names a real omission, since the statement gives no timeline, but the vocabulary is vague ('a structural concern') rather than technical, and the missing timeline is not what the style works to keep from view. (C) misreads the tone, since 'The Department appreciates the community's patience' is formal courtesy, not shared frustration, and the detour's distance is given ('0.6 miles south'). (D) misdescribes the sentences, which are long and measured and work to calm readers, and sentence 2 does report the 2023 finding.
parts.n: STL-1.Q (style is the mix of word choice, syntax, and conventions), skill 7.A. Thinking: judge what a source's style lets it do and what it keeps from view. Trap: (A), which takes official diction as proof of authority.

parts.q:
Each of the following describes a real difference between the styles of the two passages EXCEPT:
(A) Passage 1 mostly uses verbs that leave out who acted, while Passage 2 names who did what, starting with the writer.
(B) Passage 1 relies on abstract nouns such as 'concern' and 'findings,' while Passage 2 relies on concrete physical details.
(C) Passage 1 uses a parenthetical element to supply information, while Passage 2 uses no parenthetical element at all.
(D) Passage 1 keeps a formal distance from its readers, while Passage 2 speaks to them in a personal, conversational voice.
parts.a: (C). Passage 2 does use a parenthetical: '(three-eighths of an inch, she informed me, with some pride).' Both passages interrupt a sentence with information the sentence could do without, though to different ends: Passage 1's '(0.6 miles south)' serves residents' practical needs, while Passage 2's adds a precise measurement and a moment of warmth that keeps the complaint personal. (A) is a real difference: apart from 'The Department appreciates,' Passage 1's verbs hide the actor ('has been closed,' 'was noted'), against 'I walked' and 'I reported.' (B) is real: 'structural concern' and 'findings' against a crack 'under the third lamppost' and a school ruler. (D) is real: 'The Department appreciates' against 'she informed me, with some pride.'
parts.n: STL-1.T (parenthetical elements supply information that serves the audience or the purpose), skill 7.B. Thinking: test each claimed difference against both texts. Trap: (A), chosen by students who notice 'The Department appreciates' and overlook that nearly every other verb in Passage 1 hides its actor.

parts.q:
A student claims: 'Passage 1 is objective because it avoids descriptive words and never uses the word I; only Passage 2 reveals a point of view.' Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) The claim is correct, because an official statement that avoids the first person conveys no attitude toward its subject.
(B) The claim is correct, because Passage 2's personal details make it an opinion piece, while Passage 1 reports only facts.
(C) The claim is incorrect, because Passage 1 exaggerates the danger of the bridge in order to justify its sudden closure.
(D) The claim is incorrect, because Passage 1 does use descriptive words, such as 'minor,' that convey a point of view.
parts.a: (D). The student's premise is false. Passage 1 calls the earlier cracking 'minor' and 'surface' and its caution an 'abundance,' words that describe and also judge, playing down the earlier finding and presenting the closure as generous. Avoiding 'I' removes the speaker from view, not the perspective. (A) assumes that impersonal writing is neutral, the very assumption the passage's style relies on. (B) is half right about Passage 2, which is openly personal, but wrong that Passage 1 reports only facts; 'out of an abundance of caution' is a characterization. (C) reverses Passage 1's tendency, which is to minimize the danger, not to exaggerate it.
parts.n: STL-1.B (descriptive words convey a perspective toward what they describe), skill 7.A. Thinking: test a claim about objectivity against the descriptive words actually in the text. Trap: (B), which is right about one passage and wrong about the other.

mc.stem:
Questions 14-19 refer to the following.

The following passage is from an essay by a court reporter, the person who makes the official written record of everything said aloud in a courtroom. The essay appeared in a collection of essays about work. The sentences are numbered. (Written for practice; the writer and the collection are invented.)

(1) For nineteen years my job has been to write down everything anyone says aloud in Courtroom 4B, and to write down nothing else. (2) I do not record the way a witness's voice drops when she reaches the part about the car, or the way a defendant's mother holds her purse in both hands, or the long silence after a verdict. (3) The record does not want those things; the record wants words.

(4) But the record is not as bare as it looks. (5) A transcript has no tone of voice, so it borrows one from punctuation, and every mark I type is a small decision about what someone meant. (6) Consider a witness who says, "I didn't see him I heard him." (7) If I type "I didn't see him; I heard him," she is correcting a detail, calmly, the way you might correct a date. (8) If I type "I didn't see him—I heard him," she is catching herself in the middle of a thought, and a juror who reads the transcript may wonder what made her change course. (9) The words are the same. (10) The witness is not.

(11) Lawyers know this, and the best of them read transcripts the way jewelers read stones, turning each sentence under the light. (12) Once, during an appeal, two attorneys argued for most of an afternoon about a comma I had not typed. (13) The witness had said, according to my record, "I didn't leave because he threatened me." (14) With a comma after "leave," her sentence says that she stayed and that the threat was the reason; without one, it can also mean that she did leave, but not because of the threat. (15) I had heard no pause, and so I typed no comma. (16) I still believe there was none. (17) But no one can prove the absence of a pause, and I have never forgotten that an appeal turned, for one afternoon, on a mark I chose not to make.

(18) People sometimes ask whether the work is boring. (19) It is not boring; it is lonely. (20) Everyone else in the room is allowed a reaction. (21) The judge frowns, the jurors lean forward, the family in the second row weeps or does not. (22) I type. (23) And yet the longer I do this job, the less I believe that I am the one person in the room without a point of view. (24) Mine is simply smaller than theirs and harder to see: it lives in the commas.

parts.q:
Sentences 9 and 10 ('The words are the same. The witness is not.') chiefly serve to
(A) compress sentences 6-8 into two short, parallel sentences, so that the change falls on the person the record shows
(B) concede that punctuation cannot change what a witness's words mean, only how a juror happens to feel about the witness
(C) suggest that the witness in sentences 6-8 changed her testimony between the first transcript and the second one
(D) move the essay from its general claims about transcripts to the particular story of the appeal that comes next
parts.a: (A). Sentences 6-8 show two transcriptions of identical words producing two different witnesses, one calm and one catching herself. Sentences 9-10 reduce that demonstration to a pair of short, matched sentences whose second half overturns the first: the words hold still, and the person a reader meets in the record changes. The brevity and the parallel structure make the claim quotable and final. (B) reverses the point; the essay says punctuation changes what readers take someone to have meant. (C) reads the example as two events, but the essay describes one utterance typed two possible ways. (D) misplaces the transition, which comes in sentence 11 with 'Lawyers know this.'
parts.n: STL-1.H (the arrangement of sentences can emphasize ideas), with STL-1.J, skill 7.B. Thinking: explain what two short, parallel sentences do after a longer demonstration. Trap: (B), which inverts the essay's claim about punctuation.

parts.q:
In sentences 13-14, whether a comma follows 'leave' changes what the witness's sentence can mean. Which of the following sentences would be open to the same kind of dispute?
(A) "She kept the letter because she wanted to read it again."
(B) "He didn't sign the lease because the landlord pressured him."
(C) "They called the police when the front window broke."
(D) "I left the party a little after the music stopped."
parts.a: (B). The witness's sentence is ambiguous because it combines a negation ('didn't') with a 'because' clause: the 'because' clause can explain why she did not leave, or the negation can deny only the reason ('I left, but not because he threatened me'). A comma after 'leave' settles it in favor of the first reading. 'He didn't sign the lease because the landlord pressured him' has the same shape: with a comma after 'lease,' he refused to sign under pressure; without one, it can also mean he signed, but not because of the pressure. (A) has 'because' but no negation, so a comma would change the rhythm but not the meaning. (C) and (D) have no negation either; a comma before 'when' or 'after' would add a pause, not a second reading.
parts.n: STL-1.N (punctuation shows the relationships among ideas in a sentence), skill 7.C. Thinking: find the structure that made the comma matter and recognize it in a new sentence. Trap: (A), which matches the 'because' but misses the negation that creates the ambiguity.

parts.q:
Sentences 23-24 refine the view of the writer's work presented in sentences 1-3 chiefly by
(A) revealing that the writer has quietly been adding her own opinions of witnesses to the transcripts she types
(B) reversing the writer's earlier claim that the record wants only words, since she now says it wants reactions too
(C) admitting that the writer, who claimed to record 'nothing else,' puts her own judgment into the record she types
(D) confirming that the writer has no point of view, since her perspective is too small for anyone in the room to notice
parts.a: (C). Sentence 1 presents the job as recording words 'and nothing else.' The essay's account of punctuation shows that every mark is 'a small decision about what someone meant,' and sentences 23-24 draw the consequence for the writer herself: she is not 'the one person in the room without a point of view'; hers 'lives in the commas.' The tone moves from matter-of-fact description to quiet confession, refining her opening rather than reversing it. (A) turns a point about punctuation into misconduct; nothing suggests she adds opinions. (B) overstates: she never says the record should include reactions, only that her judgment already enters it. (D) misreads 'smaller than theirs and harder to see,' which describes how her point of view exists, not a denial that it does.
parts.n: STL-1.F (a shift in tone can signal a refinement of perspective), skill 7.A. Thinking: trace how an ending qualifies an opening claim without contradicting it. Trap: (B), which takes a refinement for a reversal.

parts.q:
In light of sentences 6-8, the punctuation of sentence 19 ('It is not boring; it is lonely.') presents the writer as
(A) catching herself in the middle of a thought, as the witness does in the version with a dash
(B) unsure which word best describes her work, since the two clauses are given equal weight
(C) insisting that loneliness matters less than boredom, since it comes second in the sentence
(D) correcting a mistaken assumption calmly, as the witness does in the version with a semicolon
parts.a: (D). Sentence 7 says the semicolon version presents a witness 'correcting a detail, calmly.' Sentence 19 has the same shape, a denial and a correction joined by a semicolon, and it corrects the questioner's assumption ('whether the work is boring') in the same composed way. The two independent clauses set the wrong word and the right one side by side. (A) gives the semicolon the effect the essay assigns to the dash. (B) mistakes the balance of coordination for indecision; the first clause denies and the second asserts. (C) reverses the emphasis: the correcting clause, 'it is lonely,' comes last and carries the point.
parts.n: STL-1.J (coordination sets ideas side by side), with STL-1.O on punctuation and tone, skill 7.B. Thinking: apply the essay's own account of punctuation to the writer's sentence about herself. Trap: (A), which confuses the two marks the essay contrasts.

parts.q:
The colon in sentence 24 chiefly serves to
(A) withhold where her point of view lies until the last words, which tie it to the essay's account of punctuation
(B) introduce a list of the opinions the writer has formed about the people in the courtroom during her nineteen years there
(C) mark a shift from the essay's personal voice to the formal, impersonal language of the transcripts she types each day
(D) separate two independent ideas of equal weight, in the same way that the semicolons elsewhere in the essay do
parts.a: (A). The clause before the colon says the writer's point of view is 'smaller than theirs and harder to see'; the colon promises an explanation and delays it to the final words, 'it lives in the commas,' which return the confession to the essay's subject. (B) misreads the colon as introducing a list; what follows is a single clause, and the essay never names her opinions. (C) is wrong because the final clause is as personal and figurative as anything in the essay. (D) confuses the colon with the semicolon: the essay's semicolons balance equal clauses ('It is not boring; it is lonely'), while this colon makes the second clause explain the first.
parts.n: STL-1.O (punctuation advances purpose by clarifying, organizing, or emphasizing), skill 7.C. Thinking: explain what a colon does that a semicolon would not, in context. Trap: (D), which treats all punctuation between independent clauses as interchangeable.

parts.q:
A student claims that the comparison in sentence 11 ('the way jewelers read stones, turning each sentence under the light') shows the writer's contempt for lawyers. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) The claim is correct, because 'turning each sentence' suggests that lawyers twist a witness's words to suit their clients.
(B) The claim is incorrect, because the comparison credits the best lawyers with the close attention her own work needs.
(C) The claim is correct, because the writer later mocks two attorneys for spending a whole afternoon arguing over a comma.
(D) The claim is incorrect, because the writer compares lawyers to jewelers only to suggest that lawyers are paid very well.
parts.a: (B). Jewelers examine small, valuable things closely, turning them to see flaws others would miss. The comparison, applied to 'the best of them,' credits lawyers with the same attention to small marks that the essay says every transcript demands, so the diction conveys respect, not contempt. (A) seizes on a second meaning of 'turning' that the image does not support; turning a stone under the light is inspection, not distortion. (C) misreads sentences 12-17: the writer does not mock the argument over the comma but says she has 'never forgotten' that an appeal turned on it, which takes the dispute seriously. (D) invents a point about money; nothing in the comparison concerns pay.
parts.n: STL-1.A (connotation), skill 7.A. Thinking: evaluate a claim about a writer's attitude by the connotations of the comparison and its context. Trap: (C), which reads the long afternoon as ridicule rather than as evidence that commas matter.

mc.stem:
Questions 20-25 refer to the following.

The following passage is a draft of a letter that a high school senior is writing to the editor of the school newspaper. The letter urges the school board to name the school's new greenhouse after a custodian who is retiring. (Written for practice; the writer, the school, and the custodian are invented.)

(1) Mr. Ortega has worked as a custodian at Riverside High School for thirty-one years, and in June he will retire. (2) Most students know him as the man who fixes the radiator in Room 12 every winter. (3) Fewer know that the greenhouse behind the gym still exists because of him. (4) In 2009 the district planned to tear the old greenhouse down, Mr. Ortega spent three summers repairing it on his own time. (5) He replaced forty broken panes of glass. (6) He rebuilt the rotting benches. (7) He even taught himself from library books to graft tomatoes (to join the stem of one plant to the roots of a hardier one) so that the seedlings could survive the greenhouse's cold nights. (8) Now the district is building a new greenhouse to replace the one he saved, and the school board should name it for him.

(9) Some students say that buildings should be named after donors or famous graduates. (10) The greenhouse was not saved by a donor. (11) Having grown seedlings there for three years, the greenhouse taught me patience, and it has taught hundreds of other students the same thing. (12) Naming it for Mr. Ortega would be super cool, and it would show that our school values work that is done quietly. (13) The new greenhouse opens in the fall; its name should honor the man who kept the old one alive.

parts.q:
The writer wants to revise sentence 4 (reproduced below) so that it is correctly punctuated and presents the district's plan as the background to Mr. Ortega's work rather than as an equal event.
'In 2009 the district planned to tear the old greenhouse down, Mr. Ortega spent three summers repairing it on his own time.'
Which of the following versions best accomplishes this goal?
(A) In 2009 the district planned to tear the old greenhouse down, and Mr. Ortega spent three summers repairing it on his own time.
(B) In 2009 the district planned to tear the old greenhouse down; Mr. Ortega spending three summers repairing it on his own time.
(C) When the district planned in 2009 to tear the old greenhouse down, Mr. Ortega spent three summers repairing it on his own time.
(D) In 2009 the district, planning to tear the old greenhouse down, Mr. Ortega spent three summers repairing it on his own time.
parts.a: (C). Sentence 4 joins two independent clauses with only a comma. 'When the district planned...' turns the first into a subordinate clause, which fixes the error and makes the district's plan the occasion for what the main clause reports, Mr. Ortega's three summers of work. (A) fixes the punctuation with 'and,' but coordination presents the plan and the repairs as equal events, which the goal rules out. (B) replaces the verb 'spent' with 'spending,' so the words after the semicolon are no longer an independent clause. (D) leaves 'the district' with no verb of its own, so the sentence has two subjects and a single predicate.
parts.n: STL-1.I (subordination and coordination express the intended relationship between ideas), with STL-1.G, skill 8.B. Thinking: meet two goals at once, a correct sentence and the right relationship between its ideas. Trap: (A), which is correct but coordinates what the goal says to subordinate.

parts.q:
The writer wants to combine sentences 5 and 6 (reproduced below) so that the two repairs are presented as equally important parts of Mr. Ortega's work.
'He replaced forty broken panes of glass. He rebuilt the rotting benches.'
Which of the following best accomplishes this goal?
(A) He replaced forty broken panes of glass and rebuilt the rotting benches.
(B) Replacing forty broken panes of glass, he rebuilt the rotting benches.
(C) He replaced forty broken panes of glass, rebuilding the rotting benches.
(D) Having replaced forty broken panes of glass, he rebuilt the rotting benches.
parts.a: (A). A compound predicate joined by 'and' gives the two repairs the same grammatical rank, so neither is subordinate to the other. (B) turns the first repair into a participial phrase that modifies 'he,' making it background to the second and implying the two happened at once. (C) does the reverse, reducing the second repair to a trailing phrase attached to the first. (D) makes the glass a completed step before the benches, which subordinates it and adds a sequence the writer did not state. All four are grammatical; only (A) keeps the two actions equal.
parts.n: STL-1.J (coordination shows balance between ideas), skill 8.B. Thinking: tell coordination from subordination when every option is grammatical. Trap: (C), which keeps both verbs visible but demotes the second repair to a modifier.

parts.q:
Which of the following is the best version of the portion of sentence 11 reproduced below?
'Having grown seedlings there for three years, the greenhouse taught me patience,'
(A) (as it is now)
(B) The greenhouse, having grown seedlings there for three years, taught me patience,
(C) Having grown seedlings there for three years, patience is what the greenhouse taught me,
(D) Having grown seedlings there for three years, I learned patience from the greenhouse,
parts.a: (D). The opening phrase 'Having grown seedlings there for three years' describes the writer, so the word it modifies, 'I,' must come right after it. (A) makes the greenhouse the one that grew seedlings in itself, a dangling modifier. (B) moves the phrase but still attaches it to 'the greenhouse.' (C) attaches it to 'patience,' which is no better. In (D) the rest of sentence 11 still works: 'it has taught hundreds of other students the same thing' refers back to the greenhouse.
parts.n: STL-1.S (modifiers belong next to the word they modify), skill 8.B. Thinking: find who performs the action in the opening phrase and put that word next to it. Trap: (B), which moves the phrase without changing what it modifies.

parts.q:
The writer wants to revise the portion of sentence 12 reproduced below so that its diction suits a public letter meant to persuade the school board and says precisely what naming the greenhouse would do.
'Naming it for Mr. Ortega would be super cool,'
Which of the following versions best accomplishes this goal?
(A) (as it is now)
(B) Naming it for Mr. Ortega would thank him for three summers of unpaid work,
(C) Naming it for Mr. Ortega would be an extremely nice and very thoughtful gesture,
(D) Naming it for Mr. Ortega would be something that everyone would agree with,
parts.a: (B). The letter is a public appeal to the school board, printed in the school newspaper, and slang in a request to the board makes the writer sound less serious than her case; and 'super cool' says nothing about what the naming would accomplish, so (A) fails the precision goal even for a reader who thinks slang harmless among students. 'Would thank him for three summers of unpaid work' is formal enough for the audience and precise, since it names the act being honored and recalls sentence 4's 'on his own time.' (A) keeps the slang. (C) is more formal but no more precise; 'extremely nice' and 'very thoughtful' are intensified vagueness. (D) replaces the claim with an assertion of agreement that sentence 9 has already shown to be false.
parts.n: STL-1.C (precise word choice), with STL-1.E on tone, skill 8.A. Thinking: judge revisions against two criteria at once, register and precision. Trap: (C), which fixes the register but not the vagueness.

parts.q:
The writer is considering deleting the parenthetical element in sentence 7 (reproduced below).
'(to join the stem of one plant to the roots of a hardier one)'
Should the writer keep or delete it?
(A) Keep it, because it explains a term many readers may not know, which shows how much he had to teach himself.
(B) Keep it, because it provides the only proof in the letter that Mr. Ortega is the one who actually saved the greenhouse.
(C) Delete it, because parentheses are too informal for a letter that is meant to be printed in the school newspaper.
(D) Delete it, because it interrupts the account of Mr. Ortega's work with a definition that belongs in a science class.
parts.a: (A). Few readers of a school newspaper will know what grafting involves, and the parenthetical tells them in a phrase. That serves the letter's purpose: once readers see what the technique requires, the fact that he learned it 'from library books' becomes evidence of the effort the letter wants honored. (B) overstates its function; the parenthetical defines a term and proves nothing about who saved the greenhouse, which sentences 3-6 establish. (C) states a rule that does not exist; parentheses are a standard way to add supplementary information. (D) treats the definition as a digression, but it supports the very claim sentence 7 makes.
parts.n: STL-1.T (parenthetical elements address the audience's needs and advance the purpose), skill 8.B. Thinking: decide whether an interruption serves this audience and this purpose. Trap: (D), which judges the parenthetical by its subject rather than its function in the letter.

parts.q:
The writer wants to combine sentences 9 and 10 (reproduced below) so that the objection is acknowledged but the writer's reply receives the emphasis.
'Some students say that buildings should be named after donors or famous graduates. The greenhouse was not saved by a donor.'
Which of the following best accomplishes this goal?
(A) Some students say that buildings should be named after donors or famous graduates, and the greenhouse was not saved by a donor.
(B) Some students say that buildings should be named after donors or famous graduates because the greenhouse was not saved by a donor.
(C) Although some students say that buildings should be named after donors or famous graduates, the greenhouse was not saved by a donor.
(D) Although the greenhouse was not saved by a donor, some students say that buildings should be named after donors or famous graduates.
parts.a: (C). 'Although' places the objection in a subordinate clause, acknowledging it, and leaves the reply in the main clause, where the emphasis falls: this greenhouse was saved by a custodian, not a donor. (A) coordinates the two, so the reply carries no more weight than the objection it answers. (B) makes the reply the reason for the objection, which reverses the logic. (D) subordinates the reply and puts the objection in the main clause, giving the emphasis to the wrong side.
parts.n: STL-1.K (subordination shows an imbalance between ideas), skill 8.B. Thinking: put the idea that should dominate in the main clause. Trap: (D), which uses 'Although' but attaches it to the wrong idea.

fr.title: Rhetorical analysis: an arborist tells a town its oldest oak must come down
fr.stem:
In 2025, the city arborist of a small city published the following letter in the local newspaper, two weeks before her crew was scheduled to remove a white oak more than two hundred years old that stood in the center of the town square. More than three thousand residents had signed a petition asking the city to save the tree. (The arborist, the city, and the tree are invented for practice; an exam passage runs 600 to 800 words.)

Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the arborist makes to convey her message to the residents who signed the petition.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
• Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

To the people of Carrow Falls:

I have climbed the Commons Oak more times than anyone alive. I know where the lightning scar from 1961 runs under the bark, which limb the children call the Saddle, and how the crown sounds in a west wind, a little like surf. So I want you to hear this from me, and not from a work order: on the morning of October 14, my crew will take the oak down.

I have read your petition. All 3,112 names. Many of you asked whether we could cable the limbs, or fence off the trunk, or simply wait. Those are the right questions. They are the questions I asked first.

Here are the answers. Last spring we drilled into the trunk in six places and measured the wood inside. Four feet above the ground, less than a third of it is still sound; the rest is hollow or soft. A tree that size can stand for a long time on a thin shell, until one afternoon it cannot. Cables hold limbs, not trunks. A fence would keep people away from the base of the tree but not from the eighty feet of it that would come down across the square, the bandstand, and the Saturday market. And waiting is what we have been doing, carefully, for eleven years.

I will not tell you it is only a tree. It is not. It is where your parents told you to meet them if you got lost, and where some of you got engaged, and where the town gathered the night the mill closed. When it comes down, the square will look wrong for a long time, and it should.

But I would ask you to do one more thing with the love you put into that petition. Last fall we gathered four hundred acorns from the Commons Oak. They are sprouting now in the city nursery, in paper cups that your children labeled with their names at the harvest fair. In April we will plant the strongest of them where its parent stood. It will be a stick with three leaves. It will not shade anyone for thirty years.

Come and help us plant it anyway. That is how the first one got there.

Ruth Adair
City Arborist

rows.earns: A defensible thesis that analyzes the arborist's rhetorical choices in light of her purpose and audience, for example: 'Writing to residents who expect a city official to dismiss their grief, the arborist first proves she knows the oak as intimately as they do, then answers their petition in short, flat sentences of fact, and finally grieves with them before turning that grief toward planting the tree's offspring, so that the removal reads as a loss she shares and the invitation as the one thing left to do.' The thesis may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('the arborist uses rhetorical choices to convey her message'); naming devices with no purpose ('she uses imagery, repetition, and short sentences'); summarizing the letter; or arguing about whether the tree should be cut down instead of analyzing her choices.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how multiple choices serve her purpose: the precise, sensory opening ('the lightning scar from 1961,' 'the Saddle,' the crown that sounds 'a little like surf') establishes that she loves the tree as the petitioners do, so the colon that delivers the news lands as word from a friend, 'not from a work order'; the fragment 'All 3,112 names' and 'Those are the right questions' honor the petition before refusing it; the answers come in short declaratives ('Cables hold limbs, not trunks') and a single number ('less than a third of it is still sound') that leave no room for hope without sounding cold; the repeated 'and where' in the fourth paragraph grants the tree's meaning in the residents' own memories, and 'the square will look wrong for a long time, and it should' validates their grief; and the shift to the acorns, the 'stick with three leaves,' and 'Come and help us plant it anyway' redirects the energy of the petition into an act, closing on a line that places the residents where the town's first planters stood.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence for every claim, but commentary explains only some choices, or explains one well and lists the rest. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it ('this shows she cares about the tree'), or no line of reasoning joins the paragraphs. 1: mostly general evidence and a summary of the letter. 0: restates the thesis, repeats the passage, or is irrelevant. Labeling the opening 'ethos' without explaining what it lets the later refusal do stays at 2 or below.

rows.earns: A consistently complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, for example explaining the tension she must manage (she must carry out the act her readers petitioned against while keeping their trust) and how her shifts in tone resolve it, from intimate memory to flat fact to shared grief to invitation; or explaining the significance of the final sentence, which recasts the loss as the oak's own history repeating, so that the residents who mourn the tree become the people who replace it; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: A closing sentence calling the letter 'very effective'; a general claim about trees or civic life; a tension named once and dropped; or elevated vocabulary that carries no insight. The point rewards the essay's thinking throughout, not a final flourish.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that analyzes the arborist's choices and explains how they serve her purpose with these readers.
parts.a: Model: 'Knowing that the petitioners expect an official to overrule them, the arborist proves she loves the oak as they do, answers each of their proposals in plain, unarguable facts, and then honors their grief before giving it somewhere to go, so that her decision reads not as the city's refusal but as a loss she asks them to turn into a planting.' It names the audience's expectation, her main moves in the order she makes them, and the purpose they serve.
parts.n: 'The arborist uses imagery, statistics, and repetition to persuade the residents' lists devices with no function and does not earn the point.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs in a line of reasoning, each with evidence and the commentary that explains how the choices serve her purpose.
parts.a:
¶1 Earning the right to deliver bad news: the sensory, specific knowledge of the tree ('the lightning scar from 1961,' 'the Saddle,' 'a little like surf'), then 'So I want you to hear this from me, and not from a work order,' and the colon that holds the news until the end of the sentence. Commentary: the details prove an intimacy that matches the petitioners' own, so the news comes from someone who shares the loss; the colon makes readers wait for the news until she has placed herself beside them.
¶2 Answering the petition without dismissing it: 'All 3,112 names,' 'Those are the right questions,' then the short declaratives of the third paragraph ('Cables hold limbs, not trunks') and the measured figure ('less than a third of it is still sound'). Commentary: the fragment counts the names as she has read them; granting that the questions were right makes the answers a shared inquiry rather than a rebuttal; the plain, short sentences leave no room for false hope and no trace of condescension.
¶3 Turning grief into an act: the repeated 'and where' memories, 'the square will look wrong for a long time, and it should,' then the acorns, the 'stick with three leaves,' and 'Come and help us plant it anyway. That is how the first one got there.' Commentary: she grants the tree's meaning in the residents' own memories before asking anything of them; the modest image of the seedling refuses to pretend the loss is made good; and the closing line makes the planting the town's own history repeating, so the petitioners become the oak's next planters.
parts.n: Paragraphs organized by device ('the imagery paragraph, the statistics paragraph') tend to list; organize by what she does to her readers, in the order she does it, and explain each step.

parts.q: Row C plan: explain how this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Carry the central tension through every paragraph: the arborist must do what her readers asked her not to do and still keep their trust. Show how each shift in tone manages it (intimacy makes her credible, flat facts make the decision final, shared grief keeps her on the residents' side), and end by explaining how the last line reframes the removal as part of the tree's own story, so that the choice the residents face is no longer whether to lose the oak but whether to help plant the next one.
parts.n: Ending with 'this letter teaches us the importance of nature' gestures at a broader idea without analyzing the arborist's choices, and earns nothing.

fr.title: Style and accountability: the footbridge passages
fr.stem:
Reread the two passages about the footbridge from questions 8-13, reproduced below, and answer the questions that follow.

The two passages below concern the closing of a footbridge. Passage 1 is a statement posted on a city's website by its department of public works. Passage 2 is from a post on a neighborhood association's blog, written by a resident two days later. The sentences of each passage are numbered. (Written for practice; the city, the writers, and the bridge are invented.)

Passage 1

(1) The Mill Street Footbridge has been closed to all pedestrian and bicycle traffic, effective immediately, following the identification of a structural concern during a scheduled inspection on May 12. (2) Although minor surface cracking was noted during the 2023 inspection, the bridge remained within established safety guidelines until last week's findings. (3) The closure has been undertaken out of an abundance of caution. (4) Residents are advised to use the Elm Street Bridge (0.6 miles south) as an alternate route. (5) An engineering assessment is underway, and further information will be provided as it becomes available. (6) The Department appreciates the community's patience and remains committed to the safety of all residents.

Passage 2

(1) On Tuesday morning I walked my daughter to school the way we always go, across the Mill Street footbridge, and found it wrapped in orange fencing. (2) One sign said CLOSED. (3) Another said that the city apologized for any inconvenience. (4) The city's statement, posted that afternoon, says that a "structural concern" was "identified" on May 12. (5) I would like to identify it more precisely. (6) It is a crack in the concrete under the third lamppost, and it is not new. (7) I reported it to the city's hotline in April 2023, when it was as thin as a pencil line, and again last fall, when I could lay my daughter's school ruler in it (three-eighths of an inch, she informed me, with some pride). (8) Both times I received a polite email thanking me for my report.

(9) I am glad the bridge is closed. (10) I would rather walk the extra mile to Elm Street every morning than cross a bridge that is coming apart. (11) But I would like the city to stop describing its caution as abundant. (12) Abundant caution would have looked at the crack when a resident first pointed to it. (13) What the city showed was caution at the last possible moment, which is a different thing, and a smaller one.

parts.q: In sentences 1 and 7 of Passage 2, the writer mentions her daughter. Explain how these details contribute to the writer's tone and to her purpose.
parts.a: The daughter gives the complaint stakes and a steady, reasonable tone. In sentence 1 she shows what the bridge is for, a child's daily walk to school, so the danger is concrete. In sentence 7 the parenthetical '(three-eighths of an inch, she informed me, with some pride)' adds warmth and a light touch of humor, which keeps the post from sounding like a rant and makes its criticism more credible: the writer is a careful parent who measured the crack, not an angry neighbor. It also sharpens the point quietly, since a child with a school ruler could see what the city's inspections did not act on.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the daughter adds pathos' or 'makes readers feel sympathy' with no account of the tone the details create or how they serve the complaint; or the misreading that the writer blames the city for inconveniencing her daughter.

parts.q: A student argues that Passage 2 would persuade the city's department of public works more effectively if it used the same formal, impersonal style as Passage 1. Do you agree? Justify your answer with reference to the writer's purpose and at least one specific stylistic choice.
parts.a: Disagree, largely. The writer's purpose is to establish that the city knew about the crack long before May 12, and her first-person, dated sentences do that work: 'I reported it to the city's hotline in April 2023,' 'and again last fall,' 'Both times I received a polite email.' An impersonal style ('a crack was reported') would hide who knew what and when, which is exactly the evasion she criticizes in Passage 1. A qualified answer also earns the point, for example that a formal complaint to the department might drop the humor of the ruler, provided it explains why the first-person, specific record of reports must stay.
parts.n: Earns nothing: agreeing because 'formal writing is always more persuasive' with no reference to her purpose; or disagreeing with only 'her personal voice is more interesting,' naming no choice and no purpose.

parts.q: Explain how the structure of sentence 13 of Passage 2 ('What the city showed was caution at the last possible moment, which is a different thing, and a smaller one.') conveys the writer's judgment of the city.
parts.a: The sentence first renames the city's 'abundance of caution' as 'caution at the last possible moment,' then adds two short phrases after commas that deliver the verdict in steps: 'a different thing' (it is not the kind of caution the city claims) and 'a smaller one' (it is less of it). Placing 'a smaller one' last answers 'abundant' with its opposite in the final, emphatic position, and the quiet understatement makes the judgment sound measured rather than angry, which is more damaging to the city than an outburst would be.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the sentence is long and shows the writer is upset'; or identifying the sentence as a comparison without explaining how its order and its final phrase answer the city's word 'abundant.'

fr.title: Sentence craft: how structure assigns responsibility
fr.stem:
A school district has cut its high school library's budget, and the library will now close on Fridays. Three writers report these facts in a single sentence. (The district, the school, and the writers are invented for practice.)

Version A, from the district's newsletter: 'The district cut the library's budget by twelve percent, and the library will close on Fridays.'
Version B, from the principal's letter to families: 'Because the district cut the library's budget by twelve percent, the library will close on Fridays.'
Version C, from a student's letter to the school board: 'The library will close on Fridays, although the district cut its budget by only twelve percent.'

parts.q: Explain how Versions A and B present the relationship between the budget cut and the Friday closing differently.
parts.a: Version A coordinates: two independent clauses joined by 'and' set the cut and the closing side by side as equal facts and leave the connection between them to the reader. Version B subordinates: the cut sits in a 'because' clause and the closing in the main clause, so the sentence asserts that the cut caused the closing and makes the closing the news.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'Version B is longer' or 'Version B uses a transition' without explaining what 'because' asserts that 'and' does not.

parts.q: Explain why the district might prefer Version A for its newsletter while the principal chooses Version B, and justify your answer by referring to what each structure asserts.
parts.a: Version B states that the district's cut caused the closing, so it assigns responsibility to the district, which suits a principal who wants families to see the closing as forced on the school rather than chosen by it. Version A reports both facts without saying one caused the other, which lets the district announce its cut and the closing without stating that it is responsible for the second. Each writer chooses the structure that places responsibility where that writer wants it.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the district wants to be clear and the principal wants to be persuasive,' which names no difference in what the structures assert; or the claim that Version A is simply more concise.

parts.q: The student hopes Version C will persuade the board to reconsider. Predict how board members are likely to read the sentence, and justify your prediction by explaining how the words 'although' and 'only' shape its meaning.
parts.a: Board members are likely to read Version C as an argument that the closing is out of proportion to the cut. 'Although' sets the two facts against each other, implying that the cut does not justify the closing, and 'only,' placed before 'twelve percent,' shrinks the cut, so the sentence suggests that a modest cut produced a drastic response. The student's sentence may therefore redirect the board's attention from the district's cut to the school's choice to close on Fridays, which helps if the student wants the board to press for another solution but could backfire if the board sees the closing as the school's decision rather than its own. Any prediction earns the point if it is justified through both words.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'the board will be persuaded because the student sounds upset'; or an explanation of 'although' alone that ignores what 'only' does to the size of the cut.
